By hand
B1. Bisection on \(x^2 = 3\). Let \(f(x) = x^2 - 3\) on \([1, 2]\). (a) Check that \([1, 2]\) is a bracket. (b) Do four bisection steps. Write a table with \(a\), \(b\), \(m\), \(f(m)\) and the new bracket. (c) After four steps, what is your estimate of \(\sqrt3\), and what error bound can you guarantee? Compare with \(\sqrt 3 = 1.7320508\). (d) How many steps guarantee a bracket narrower than \(10^{-6}\)? Than \(10^{-12}\)?

For \(H = 10\), give the narrowest brackets the table allows. Which way does the stock change (grow or shrink) between the two roots?
How many bisection steps from each bracket give a width below \(10^{-6}\)?
For \(H = 15\) there is no sign change. Does that prove that \(f\) has no root? What would you do to be sure? What does it mean for the fish?
Why is \([0, 100]\) useless as a starting bracket for \(H = 10\), although it contains both roots?

B3. Tolerances in floating point. (a) A cell population model has a steady state near \(3\times10^8\) cells. You run bisection on \([0, 10^9]\) with the absolute rule “stop when \(b - a < 10^{-8}\)”. The gap between doubles near \(x\) is \(2^{\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor - 52}\), and \(2^{28} \approx 2.7\times10^8\). Will the loop ever stop? How many steps does the relative rule \(b - a < 10^{-10}\,|m|\) take instead? (b) A binding equation has its root at a free ligand concentration of \(2\times10^{-9}\) M. You bisect on \([0, 10^{-6}]\) M with the rule \(b - a < 10^{-8}\cdot\max(1, |m|)\). How many steps are taken, and how many correct digits does the answer have? Suggest two fixes.
B4. Beverton–Holt by hand. \(N_{t+1} = \dfrac{R N_t}{1 + (R-1)N_t/K}\) with \(R = 3\), \(K = 100\), \(N_0 = 50\). (a) Compute \(N_1, \dots, N_4\). (b) Compute the errors \(e_t = K - N_t\) and the ratios \(e_{t+1}/e_t\). What do they approach? (c) Show that \(g'(N) = \dfrac{R}{(1 + (R-1)N/K)^2}\), and that \(g'(K) = 1/R\). Compare with (b). (d) Let \(u_t = 1/N_t\). Show that \(u_{t+1} = \dfrac{u_t}{R} + \dfrac{R-1}{RK}\), so the error \(u_t - 1/K\) is divided by exactly \(R\) each year. Check with your numbers.
B5. Cobwebs of straight lines. Each map has the fixed point \(x^* = 2\): (a) \(g(x) = 1 + 0.5x\), (b) \(g(x) = 3 - 0.5x\), (c) \(g(x) = -1 + 1.5x\), (d) \(g(x) = 5 - 1.5x\). For each, compute \(x_1, x_2, x_3\) from \(x_0 = 3\), sketch the cobweb plot, and say whether the iteration converges, and whether monotonically or alternating. Why is \(e_{k+1} = g'(x^*)\,e_k\) exact here?
B6. Ricker stability. \(g(N) = N e^{r(1 - N/K)}\). (a) Use the product rule to show \(g'(N) = e^{r(1-N/K)}\,(1 - rN/K)\), and \(g'(K) = 1 - r\). (b) Classify the steady state \(N^* = K\) for \(r = 0.5\), \(1\), \(1.5\), \(1.9\) and \(2.5\): attracting or repelling, monotone or alternating. Which \(r\) gives the fastest return to \(K\)? (c) With \(K = 100\), \(r = 1.5\) and \(N_0 = 50\), compute \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) (\(e^{0.75} = 2.117\), \(e^{-0.0878} = 0.916\)). Does the sign of the error behave as (b) predicts? (d) A disturbance moves the stock 10 below \(K\). Roughly how many years until it is within 0.01 of \(K\), for \(r = 0.5\) and for \(r = 1.9\)?
B7. Four ways to write one equation. The equation \(x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0\) has the roots \(3\) and \(-1\). It can be rearranged as \(x = g(x)\) with (a) \(g_a(x) = \sqrt{2x + 3}\), (b) \(g_b(x) = (x^2 - 3)/2\), (c) \(g_c(x) = 3/(x - 2)\), (d) \(g_d(x) = 2 + 3/x\). Check that 3 is a fixed point of each. Compute \(g'(3)\) and \(g'(-1)\) for each and predict which iterations converge to which root, and at what rate. Which form would you pick for the root 3, and which for \(-1\)?
B8. Read an iteration. A fixed-point iteration gives \(x_0 = 10.000\), \(x_1 = 10.800\), \(x_2 = 11.440\), \(x_3 = 11.952\). (a) Compute the steps \(d_k = x_{k+1} - x_k\) and their ratios. Estimate \(L = g'(x^*)\). (b) Estimate the remaining error of \(x_3\) and the fixed point \(x^*\). (c) The stopping rule is \(|d_k| < 10^{-6}\). About how many more steps will be taken, and what is the true error at that point?

title: Exercise: bisection and fixed-point iteration
text:
In code
Write and run each task in R, Python or Rust. Use the model from the Background.
C1. Bisection. (a) Write bisect(f, a, b, tol, maxit) that checks the bracket, stops when \(b - a < \text{tol}\cdot\max(1, |m|)\), and returns the root, the number of iterations and the final bracket. (b) Test it on \(x^2 - 3\) on \([1, 2]\) with tol \(= 10^{-6}, 10^{-10}, 10^{-14}\); compare the step counts with your prediction (B1) and the errors with sqrt(3). (c) Run it with tol \(= 10^{-17}\). What happens, and what is the final bracket width? (d) Run it on \(1/(x - 1)\) on \([0, 3]\) and evaluate the function at the “root”.
C2. Both steady states of the harvested stock. (a) Evaluate \(f\) on the grid \(0, 5, \dots, 100\), find the intervals with a sign change, and bisect each to tol \(= 10^{-12}\). (b) Evaluate \(g'(N)\) at both roots and classify them. (c) For the catches \(H = 10, 12, 14, 14.2, 14.3, 15\), find all steady states on a grid with spacing 0.1. What happens as \(H\) grows? Compare with B2(c).
C3. Fixed-point iteration. (a) Write fixed_point(g, x0, tol, maxit) that stops when \(|x_{k+1} - x_k| < \text{tol}\) and returns all iterates. (b) Run it on the population map \(g\) from \(N_0 = 30\) and from \(N_0 = 21\), and on the rearrangements \(g_2(N) = K\left(1 - \log(1 + H/N)/r\right)\) and \(g_3(N) = H/(e^{r(1 - N/K)} - 1)\) from 30. For each, print the number of steps, the root, the rate \(L\) estimated from the last two steps, and the estimated remaining error \(|d|\,L/(1-L)\). (c) Compare the estimated error of the population map with the true error, using the bisection root as reference. (d) What happens from \(N_0 = 20\)?
C4. Error against iteration. For 60 iterations, record the error of bisection on \([50, 100]\) (use the bound \((b-a)/2\)), of the population map \(g\) and of \(g_2\) (both from 30), all against the upper root. Plot them on a log-\(y\) axis. Fit the slope of \(\log_{10}(\text{error})\) against \(k\), using only errors between \(10^{-12}\) and \(10^{-2}\), and compare with \(\log_{10}\) of \(\tfrac12\), \(|g'(N^*)|\) and \(|g_2'(N^*)|\), where \(g_2'(N) = KH/(rN(N+H))\).
C5. Ricker regimes. For \(r = 0.5, 1.5, 1.9, 2.3, 2.6, 3.0\) (no harvest, \(K = 100\), \(N_0 = 20\)), iterate 1000 years, then record the next 64 values. How many distinct values (rounded to 6 decimals) are there? Relate to \(g'(K) = 1 - r\). Draw a cobweb plot for \(r = 1.5\) (R or Python).
C6. Chaos and rounding. \(N e^{r(1 - N/K)}\) and \(N e^{r} e^{-rN/K}\) are equal in exact arithmetic. Iterate both from \(N_0 = 20\) for 100 years with \(r = 1.5\) and with \(r = 3\), and print their difference after 1, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 years. What do you conclude about long chaotic simulations? Does your C5 output for \(r = 3\) agree with someone else’s in another language?
C7. The library routine. Find both steady states with uniroot (Python: brentq; Rust: argmin’s BrentRoot), first with the default tolerance and then with a tight one. Compare the errors and the numbers of iterations with your bisection (C1, B2). Then try \(H = 15\) on \([0, 100]\).

title: Exercise: bisection and fixed-point iteration
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — bisection by hand (B1, B2)





Keep the half whose endpoints have \(f\) of opposite signs: if \(f(m)\) has the sign of \(f(a)\), the new bracket is \([m, b]\), otherwise \([a, m]\). The estimate is the midpoint of the last bracket, with error at most half its width. Steps: the smallest \(k\) with \((b - a)/2^k < \text{tol}\); \(2^{10} \approx 10^3\), so \(10^{-6}\) needs about 20 halvings of an interval of length 1.









Hint 2 — tolerances (B3)





A bracket \([a, b]\) with \(a\) and \(b\) neighbouring doubles cannot be halved: the midpoint rounds to \(a\) or \(b\). So an absolute tolerance smaller than the gap near the root is never reached. For (b), compare the final bracket width with the size of the root itself.









Hint 3 — derivatives at the fixed point (B4, B6, B7)





Quotient rule: \(\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)' = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}\). Product rule for Ricker: \(\left(N\,e^{h(N)}\right)' = e^{h(N)} + N\,h'(N)\,e^{h(N)}\) with \(h(N) = r(1 - N/K)\), \(h' = -r/K\). At a fixed point, \(|g'| < 1\) means convergence with rate \(|g'|\); the number of steps to shrink an error by a factor \(F\) is about \(\log F / \log(1/|g'|)\).









Hint 4 — cobwebs (B5, C5)





From \((x_k, x_k)\) on the diagonal, go vertically to \((x_k, g(x_k))\) and then horizontally to \((x_{k+1}, x_{k+1})\) on the diagonal. For a straight line \(g(x) = c + s x\) with fixed point \(x^*\), \(g(x) - x^* = s\,(x - x^*)\) exactly. In R use segments and abline(0, 1); in Python, plt.plot([x, x, y], [x, y, y]) draws one vertical and one horizontal piece.









Hint 5 — rate and error from the steps (B8, C3)





\(d_{k+1}/d_k \approx L\). The remaining steps form a geometric series: \(x^* - x_{k+1} \approx d_k (L + L^2 + \dots) = d_k\,L/(1-L)\). In R, diff(x) gives all steps; in Python, np.diff(x). SciPy also has scipy.optimize.fixed_point, but by default it accelerates the iteration (Steffensen’s method), so it does not show the plain linear convergence of this exercise.









Hint 6 — finding sign changes on a grid (C2)





Compare the signs of neighbouring values: in R, which(sign(v[-1]) != sign(v[-length(v)])) (see sign); in Python, np.where(np.sign(v[1:]) != np.sign(v[:-1]))[0] (see np.sign). Each index \(i\) gives the bracket from grid point \(i\) to \(i+1\).









Hint 7 — fitting the slope (C4)





Fit a straight line to \(\log_{10} e_k\) against \(k\): lm(log10(e) ~ k) in R, np.polyfit(k, np.log10(e), 1) in Python. Leave out the start (not yet in the linear regime) and the floor at \(10^{-14}\) (rounding).









Hint 8 — library root finders (C7)





R: uniroot(f, c(a, b), tol = 1e-12) returns a list with $root, $iter and $estim.prec; the default tol is .Machine$double.eps^0.25. Python: brentq(f, a, b, xtol=1e-14, full_output=True) returns the root and an object with .iterations and .function_calls. Rust: Executor::new(problem, BrentRoot::new(a, b, tol)).run() from argmin; the function must be a struct implementing CostFunction.

title: Exercise: bisection and fixed-point iteration
Exercise: bisection and fixed-point iteration
text:
Where this leads

Newton and secant methods (Part 2): using the size of \(f\) and its derivative gives quadratic convergence; Newton is the fixed-point iteration \(g(x) = x - f(x)/f'(x)\), with \(g'(x^*) = 0\). Brent’s method, inside uniroot and brentq, combines those fast steps with the bisection safeguard of this exercise.
Newton for systems of equations (Part 2): steady states of models with several variables (a two-gene toggle switch), where there is no bracket and no bisection.
Equilibria, stability and the phase plane (Part 8): the continuous-time counterpart of \(|g'(N^*)| < 1\) is the sign of the eigenvalues of the Jacobian.
Optimisation in one dimension (Part 9): the maximum sustainable catch of C2 is the maximum of the surplus production, found with golden-section search, the optimisation cousin of bisection.

title: Quiz: Newton and secant methods
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of Newton’s method, the secant method and safeguarded root finding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. In one sentence: what approximation of \(f\) does Newton’s method solve at each step, and where does it come from?






Hint





Keep the first two terms of a Taylor polynomial.









Answer





The tangent line \(f(x_k) + f'(x_k)(x - x_k)\), the first-order Taylor polynomial of \(f\) at \(x_k\). Setting it to zero gives \(x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)/f'(x_k)\).




Q2. Newton’s method has error \(10^{-3}\) at some step, and \(e_{k+1} \approx 0.5\,e_k^2\). What are the errors after one and two more steps? How many steps would bisection need for the same gain?






Hint





Square, then multiply by 0.5. Bisection halves the error per step: \(\log_{10} 2 \approx 0.3\) digits.









Answer





\(0.5 \cdot 10^{-6} = 5\times10^{-7}\), then \(0.5\cdot(5\times10^{-7})^2 = 1.25\times10^{-13}\). From 3 to about 13 digits in two steps. Bisection gains 0.3 digits per step, so it needs about \(10/0.3 \approx 33\) steps for the same 10 digits.




Q3. The secant method has a lower order (1.618) than Newton (2). Why can it still be faster in practice?






Hint





Count function evaluations, not steps.









Answer





A Newton step evaluates \(f\) and \(f'\); a secant step evaluates only \(f\) (the previous value is reused). If \(f'\) costs about as much as \(f\), then per evaluation Newton has order \(\sqrt2 \approx 1.41\) and secant \(1.618\). And the secant method needs no derivative at all, which matters when \(f\) comes out of a simulation or an ODE solver.




Q4. Your hand-written Newton gives the errors \(3\times10^{-2}\), \(9\times10^{-3}\), \(2.7\times10^{-3}\), \(8\times10^{-4}\), \(2.4\times10^{-4}\). What order is this, and name two likely causes.






Hint





Look at the ratio of consecutive errors.









Answer





The ratio is constant (0.3), so this is linear convergence, not quadratic. Likely causes: a wrong derivative (Newton with the wrong \(f'\) is a fixed-point iteration with \(g'(x^*) \ne 0\); check df against a finite difference), or a multiple root where \(f'(x^*) = 0\) (Q5).




Q5. Run Newton on \(f(x) = (x - 1)^2\) from \(x_0 = 2\). What happens to the error, and why? Can uniroot find this root?






Hint





Simplify \(x - f(x)/f'(x)\) by hand first. Does \(f\) change sign?









Answer






RPythonRust


f  <- function(x) (x - 1)^2
df <- function(x) 2 * (x - 1)
x <- 2
for (k in 1:6) {
  x <- x - f(x) / df(x)
  cat(k, sprintf("%.6f", x), sprintf("%.6f", x - 1), "\n")
}

# Output:
# 1 1.500000 0.500000
# 2 1.250000 0.250000
# 3 1.125000 0.125000
# 4 1.062500 0.062500
# 5 1.031250 0.031250
# 6 1.015625 0.015625


def f(x):
    return (x - 1)**2

def df(x):
    return 2 * (x - 1)

x = 2.0
for k in range(1, 7):
    x = x - f(x) / df(x)
    print(k, f"{x:.6f}", f"{x - 1:.6f}")

# Output:
# 1 1.500000 0.500000
# 2 1.250000 0.250000
# 3 1.125000 0.125000
# 4 1.062500 0.062500
# 5 1.031250 0.031250
# 6 1.015625 0.015625


// rust/examples/newton_q5.rs  —  cargo run --example newton_q5
// Q5: Newton on a double root, f(x) = (x - 1)^2, converges only linearly.
fn main() {
    let f = |x: f64| (x - 1.0).powi(2);
    let df = |x: f64| 2.0 * (x - 1.0);
    let mut x: f64 = 2.0;
    for k in 1..=6 {
        x -= f(x) / df(x);
        println!("{} {:.6} {:.6}", k, x, x - 1.0);
    }
}

// Output:
// 1 1.500000 0.500000
// 2 1.250000 0.250000
// 3 1.125000 0.125000
// 4 1.062500 0.062500
// 5 1.031250 0.031250
// 6 1.015625 0.015625



\(x - (x-1)^2/(2(x-1)) = x - (x-1)/2\), so the error halves every step: linear convergence, exactly like bisection. At a double root \(f'(x^*) = 0\), and the quadratic-convergence argument (which divides by \(f'(x^*)\)) breaks down. uniroot and brentq cannot be used: \(f \ge 0\) everywhere, so there is no sign change to bracket. (In biology, double roots appear where two steady states merge, at a saddle-node bifurcation.)




Q6. Newton for the two-site EC50, started at \(c_0 = 10\) µM, converges in 6 steps to \(c = -3.05\) with \(f(c) = 0\) exactly. Is this a correct answer? Which check would have caught it, and what would you do instead?






Hint





What does the formula know about doses?









Answer





It is a correct root of the formula, but not of the biological problem: doses are positive. The curve is flat at \(c = 10\), so the first step is huge and lands at \(-5.73\), next to a second (meaningless) root. Checks: is the answer in the meaningful range (\(c > 0\))? A plot of \(f\) over the plausible doses shows one root, at 3.26. Fix: use a bracketing method on a positive interval (uniroot(f, c(0.01, 100))), or start closer.




Q7. uniroot(f, c(0.01, 100)) returns a root with estim.prec \(= 6.1\times10^{-5}\). What does that tell you, and what should you change?






Hint





Look up the default of the tol argument.









Answer





The root is only known to about \(6\times10^{-5}\) (absolute), because the default tol is .Machine$double.eps^0.25 \(\approx 1.2\times10^{-4}\). That is fine for reporting an EC50 to 3 digits, but not if the root is used further (a difference, a derivative, an outer optimisation). Pass tol = 1e-12 (or smaller); it costs only one or two extra evaluations. scipy.optimize.brentq has the tighter default xtol = 2e-12.




Q8. Why can Brent’s method (uniroot, brentq) not diverge or cycle, even though it uses secant-like steps?






Hint





What does it keep from bisection?









Answer





It keeps a bracket \([a, b]\) with \(f(a)f(b) < 0\) at every step. A fast step is only accepted if it lands inside the bracket and shrinks it fast enough; otherwise a bisection step is taken. The bracket therefore always contains a root and keeps shrinking, so the method converges at least about as fast as bisection, and superlinearly once the fast steps take over.




Q9. Why is a maximum-likelihood estimate a root-finding problem? What extra quantity does Newton on the score give you for free?






Hint





At a maximum, what is the derivative of the log-likelihood?









Answer





At the maximum of the log-likelihood \(\ell(\lambda)\) the derivative, the score \(S(\lambda) = \ell'(\lambda)\), is zero, so \(\hat\lambda\) is a root of \(S\). Newton needs \(S'(\lambda) = \ell''(\lambda)\); minus it at \(\hat\lambda\) is the observed information, and \(1/\sqrt{-S'(\hat\lambda)}\) is the usual standard error of \(\hat\lambda\). (Check also that \(S' < 0\) there: a root of the score could be a minimum.)




Q10. Newton’s method is a fixed-point iteration \(x_{k+1} = g(x_k)\) with \(g(x) = x - f(x)/f'(x)\). What is \(g'(x^*)\) at a simple root, and what does that say about the speed, using what you know from Bisection and fixed-point iteration?






Hint





Differentiate \(g\) with the quotient rule and use \(f(x^*) = 0\).









Answer





\(g'(x) = 1 - \dfrac{f'(x)^2 - f(x)f''(x)}{f'(x)^2} = \dfrac{f(x)f''(x)}{f'(x)^2}\), which is \(0\) at \(x^*\) since \(f(x^*) = 0\). A fixed-point iteration shrinks the error by about \(|g'(x^*)|\) per step; with \(g'(x^*) = 0\) the error shrinks faster than any fixed factor: the next term of Taylor gives \(e_{k+1} \approx \tfrac12 g''(x^*)\,e_k^2\), quadratic convergence.




Q11. Your Newton loop stops when abs(step) <= tol * abs(x), with tol = 1e-12. Give two situations where this rule alone is not enough, and what you add.






Hint





What if the iteration never settles? What if the root is 0?









Answer






If Newton diverges or cycles, the step never becomes small and the loop runs forever: add a maximum number of iterations (maxit) and a warning when it is reached, and check is.finite(). (2) If the root is at (or very near) 0, a relative test can never succeed, because \(\text{tol}\cdot|x| \to 0\): add an absolute tolerance, e.g. abs(step) <= tol * abs(x) + atol. Also check afterwards that \(|f(x)|\) is small and \(x\) is in the meaningful range.

title: Quiz: bisection and fixed-point iteration
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of bisection, fixed-point iteration and steady states of population models. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What is a bracket for a root of \(f\), and what does \(f\) need for a bracket to guarantee a root?






Hint





Think of drawing the graph of \(f\) from \((a, f(a))\) to \((b, f(b))\) without lifting the pen.









Answer





An interval \([a, b]\) where \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) have opposite signs. If \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\), the intermediate value theorem guarantees a root inside. Without continuity there is no guarantee: \(1/(x - 1)\) changes sign on \([0, 3]\) but has no root.




Q2. You bisect on the bracket \([0, 8]\) until the bracket is narrower than \(10^{-6}\). How many steps does it take, and does the answer depend on \(f\)?






Hint





After \(k\) steps the width is \(8/2^k\).









Answer





\(8/2^k < 10^{-6}\) needs \(k > \log_2(8\times10^6) = 22.9\), so 23 steps. It does not depend on \(f\) at all (as long as the bracket is valid): bisection only uses the sign of \(f\).




Q3. Your bisection returns \(x = 1.0000000009\), and you find \(f(x) \approx -10^9\). What happened, and how could you have caught it?






Hint





What can make a continuous-looking function change sign without passing through zero?









Answer





The bracket contained a pole (for example \(f(x) = 1/(x - 1)\)): \(f\) changes sign by jumping through \(\pm\infty\), and bisection closed in on the jump. Always evaluate \(f\) at the returned root (the residual) and plot \(f\) over the bracket before trusting the answer.




Q4. What do these lines do, and why?

RPythonRust


uniroot(function(x) (x - 2)^2, c(0, 5))


from scipy.optimize import brentq
brentq(lambda x: (x - 2)**2, 0, 5)


// rust/examples/bisection_fixedpoint_q4.rs  —  cargo run --example bisection_fixedpoint_q4
// Q4: a double root has no sign change, so Brent's method (argmin) refuses to start.
use argmin::core::{CostFunction, Error, Executor};
use argmin::solver::brent::BrentRoot;

struct Square;
impl CostFunction for Square {
    type Param = f64;
    type Output = f64;
    fn cost(&self, x: &f64) -> Result<f64, Error> {
        Ok((x - 2.0).powi(2)) // (x - 2)^2: root at 2, but never negative
    }
}

fn main() {
    match Executor::new(Square, BrentRoot::new(0.0, 5.0, 1e-10)).run() {
        Ok(res) => println!("{}", res),
        Err(e) => println!("{e}"),
    }
}

// Output:
// BrentRoot error: f(min) and f(max) must have different signs.









Hint





What is the sign of \((x - 2)^2\) at 0, at 5, and anywhere else?









Answer





All three stop with an error: R says f() values at end points not of opposite sign, Python raises ValueError: f(a) and f(b) must have different signs, and Rust prints BrentRoot error: f(min) and f(max) must have different signs. The function has a double root at 2: it touches zero without changing sign, so no bracketing method can find it. The harvested fish stock at its largest sustainable catch (\(H \approx 14.26\)) is exactly this case.




Q5. A fixed-point iteration has \(g'(x^*) = -0.8\). Describe what the iterates do near \(x^*\), and roughly how many steps it takes to gain one decimal digit.






Hint





\(e_{k+1} \approx g'(x^*)\,e_k\). How many factors of 0.8 make 0.1?









Answer





The iteration converges, because \(|g'(x^*)| < 1\), but the error changes sign every step: the iterates alternate above and below \(x^*\) (a spiral in the cobweb plot). The error shrinks by 0.8 per step, so one digit takes \(\log 10/\log(1/0.8) \approx 10\) steps.




Q6. The Beverton–Holt model \(N_{t+1} = R N_t/(1 + (R-1)N_t/K)\) has \(g'(K) = 1/R\). With \(R = 4\), how fast does a population return to \(K\)? Can a Beverton–Holt population ever oscillate around \(K\)?






Hint





What is the sign and size of \(1/R\) for \(R > 1\)?









Answer





Near \(K\) the deviation shrinks by a factor \(1/R = 0.25\) each year. For \(R > 1\), \(0 < 1/R < 1\), so the return is always monotone (a staircase in the cobweb plot): Beverton–Holt populations never overshoot \(K\) and never oscillate, whatever \(R\). Ricker populations can, because \(g'(K) = 1 - r\) becomes negative for \(r > 1\).




Q7. You simulate the Ricker model \(N_{t+1} = N_t e^{r(1 - N_t/K)}\) with \(r = 2.5\) and see the population alternate between two values forever. Does the steady state \(N^* = K\) still exist? Why does the simulation not find it?






Hint





Compute \(g(K)\) and \(g'(K) = 1 - r\).









Answer





Yes: \(g(K) = K e^{0} = K\) for every \(r\). But \(g'(K) = 1 - 2.5 = -1.5\), so \(|g'(K)| > 1\) and the steady state is repelling: any small deviation grows, alternating in sign, until the population settles on a 2-cycle. A bracketing root finder applied to \(g(N) - N\) still finds \(N^* = K\).




Q8. An iteration’s last three steps were \(0.100\), \(0.090\) and \(0.081\). Estimate the rate and the remaining error. If the stopping rule had been “step below \(10^{-3}\)”, how large would the error be when it stops?






Hint





The remaining error after a step \(d\) is about \(d\,L/(1 - L)\).









Answer





\(L \approx 0.9\). The remaining error is about \(0.081 \times 0.9/0.1 = 0.73\), much larger than the last step. At a step of \(10^{-3}\) the error is still about \(9\times10^{-3}\): with slow convergence the step underestimates the error by the factor \(L/(1-L) = 9\).




Q9. You simulate the harvested fish stock from 50 different starting sizes, and every run that survives ends at 74.95. A colleague concludes that 74.95 is the only steady state. What is wrong, and why does it matter?






Hint





Which steady states can a simulation (a fixed-point iteration) converge to?









Answer





A simulation only converges to attracting steady states (\(|g'| < 1\)). The unstable steady state at 20.48 (\(g' = 1.34\)) repels every run, so it never shows up, but it is the collapse threshold: below it the stock dies out even with a sustainable quota. Find it as a root of \(g(N) - N\) with bisection or uniroot on a bracket such as \([0, 50]\).




Q10. uniroot(f, c(50, 100)) returns 74.95244 for the harvested stock. How many correct digits can you expect, and what should you change?






Hint





Look up the default of tol in ?uniroot.









Answer





The default tolerance is .Machine$double.eps^0.25 \(\approx 1.2\times10^{-4}\); here the error was \(1.2\times10^{-6}\), so about 7 significant digits, and in general you are only promised about 4 decimals. Pass tol = 1e-12 (or a tolerance relative to the size of the root). scipy.optimize.brentq has tight defaults (xtol = 2e-12).




Q11. A root lies near \(x = 10^5\). Why does bisection with the absolute stopping rule \(b - a < 10^{-12}\) never stop?






Hint





The gap between neighbouring doubles near \(x\) is \(2^{\lfloor \log_2 x\rfloor - 52}\), and \(2^{16} = 65\,536\).









Answer





Near \(10^5\) the gap between doubles is \(2^{16-52} \approx 1.5\times10^{-11}\), larger than \(10^{-12}\). Once \(a\) and \(b\) are neighbouring doubles the midpoint rounds to one of them and the bracket stops shrinking, so the loop runs until maxit (or forever, if there is none). Use a relative tolerance, \(b - a < \text{tol}\cdot|m|\) with tol no smaller than about \(10^{-15}\).

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
About this lecture
Bisection is safe but slow: one binary digit per step. This lecture is about the fast methods, and about how they fail.

Newton’s method replaces f by its tangent line and solves that instead. Near a root the number of correct digits doubles every step (quadratic convergence).
The secant method uses a line through the last two points instead of the tangent, so it needs no derivative. Order about 1.6.
Both can fail: a flat derivative throws the iterate far away, a bad start runs off to a meaningless root, some starts cycle forever.
Production root finders (Brent’s method: R’s uniroot, Python’s scipy.optimize.brentq) keep a bracket for safety and take fast steps when they can.
Biology: the dose giving 50 % response of a two-site dose–response curve, and a maximum-likelihood estimate as the root of the score function.


This is the second unit of Part 2. The previous unit (Bisection and fixed-point iteration) gave us a method that always works but is slow; this one gives methods that are fast but can fail, and ends with the combination that every library uses. The two biology examples run through the whole lecture: an EC50 that has no closed form, and a maximum-likelihood estimate of a rate that has no closed form either. Both are things students already compute with black boxes (drc, nls, glm, fitdistr); here we open the box.

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
Recap: bracketing and fixed points
From Bisection and fixed-point iteration:

Bisection keeps an interval [a, b] with f(a)\,f(b) < 0 and halves it. It always converges, but only linearly: the error halves each step, about 0.3 decimal digits per step, ~50 steps for full precision.
Fixed-point iteration x_{k+1} = g(x_k) converges near x^* if |g'(x^*)| < 1, and the error shrinks by about |g'(x^*)| per step.
Stopping: stop when the step (or bracket) is below a relative tolerance, and always cap the number of steps.

Question for today: can we use more information about f (its slope) to go faster?

One slide only. Remind them of the two facts we build on: bisection is the safe fallback, and a fixed-point iteration converges at a rate set by |g’(x)|. That second fact explains Newton’s speed in a few slides: Newton is a fixed-point iteration with g’(x) = 0. In Convergence and cost we already saw Newton for sqrt(2) gain digits much faster than halving; now we see where it comes from.

title: Newton and secant methods
section: A biology problem: EC50 of a two-site drug
text:
A biology problem: EC50 of a two-site drug




A drug binds two receptor subtypes: a high-affinity site (K_1 = 0.1\,\muM, 30 % of the response) and a low-affinity site (K_2 = 5\,\muM, Hill coefficient 2, 70 %):
R(c) = 0.3\,\frac{c}{0.1 + c} + 0.7\,\frac{c^2}{25 + c^2}
Which dose c_{50} gives R = 0.5?


For one Hill curve, c_{50} = K, by algebra. For the sum of two, there is no formula: we must solve f(c) = R(c) - 0.5 = 0 numerically.


Two-site (or biphasic) dose-response curves are common: receptor subtypes, two binding sites on a protein, a drug with an on-target and an off-target effect. The single Hill curve c^n / (K^n + c^n) has c50 = K, which is why papers report EC50 as a fitted parameter. As soon as the model is a mixture, the dose that gives 50 % response is not a parameter any more and must be found by root finding. Setting R(c) = 0.5 and clearing denominators gives a quartic in c here, which has an ugly formula; for non-integer Hill coefficients there is no formula at all. Note the log dose axis, as usual in pharmacology.

title: Newton and secant methods
section: The function and its derivative in R
text:
The function and its derivative in R
R  <- function(c) 0.3 * c / (0.1 + c) + 0.7 * c^2 / (25 + c^2)
f  <- function(c) R(c) - 0.5                       # root = c50
df <- function(c) 0.03 / (0.1 + c)^2 + 35 * c / (25 + c^2)^2
f(c(1, 3, 10))
# [1] -0.2003497 -0.0243833  0.3570297

f(3) < 0 < f(10): the root lies between 3 and 10. Bisection would work.
df is f'(c), by hand: quotient rule on each term, \frac{d}{dc}\frac{c}{0.1 + c} = \frac{0.1}{(0.1 + c)^2} and \frac{d}{dc}\frac{c^2}{25 + c^2} = \frac{50c}{(25 + c^2)^2}.
Check the derivative before trusting it (exercise C1): compare with \bigl(f(c + h) - f(c)\bigr)/h.


Newton needs the derivative. Here it is short to derive by hand; the exercise asks them to check it against a finite difference, as in Convergence and cost. A wrong derivative is the single most common Newton bug: the iteration then often still converges, but only linearly, or not at all. The sign change between 3 and 10 tells us a root exists there; remember it for when Newton goes astray.

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
Newton’s idea: follow the tangent
Near x_k, Taylor says f(x) \approx f(x_k) + f'(x_k)\,(x - x_k): a straight line. Set the line to zero and solve for x:
x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac{f(x_k)}{f'(x_k)}


This is the whole derivation: keep the first two terms of Taylor (the tangent), throw away the rest, and solve the linear equation. The left panel starts at c0 = 7, on the concave side of the curve: the tangent overshoots to c1 = 1.28, but from there the tangent lands at c2 = 3.54, already close to 3.26. The right panel is the secant method, which comes later in the lecture: same idea, but with a line through the last two points. Point out that the further you are from the root, the worse the tangent approximates the curve; close to the root it is excellent.

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
One Newton step with numbers
Start at c_0 = 1:

f(1) = 0.3 \cdot \tfrac{1}{1.1} + 0.7 \cdot \tfrac{1}{26} - 0.5 = 0.27273 + 0.02692 - 0.5 = -0.20035
f'(1) = \tfrac{0.03}{1.21} + \tfrac{35}{676} = 0.02479 + 0.05178 = 0.07657
c_1 = 1 - \tfrac{-0.20035}{0.07657} = 1 + 2.6166 = 3.6166

The true c_{50} = 3.2613: from an error of 2.26 to 0.355 in one step.

Do this on the board, with a calculator. The step is minus f over f-prime: f is negative and the curve is rising, so we step to the right. The step size 2.6 is large because the slope is small. The exercise asks for the next step by hand too (on a simpler Hill curve with a known answer).

title: Newton and secant methods
section: Newton in R: watch the digits
text:
Newton in R: watch the digits
c50 <- 3.261305265055212            # converged value, see later
x <- 1
for (k in 1:5) {
  x <- x - f(x) / df(x)
  cat(k, sprintf("%.15f", x), sprintf("%.1e", abs(x - c50)), "\n")
}
# 1 3.616605460641865 3.6e-01
# 2 3.254817195760261 6.5e-03
# 3 3.261303701902960 1.6e-06
# 4 3.261305265055122 9.1e-14
# 5 3.261305265055212 0.0e+00

Correct digits: 0, 2, 6, 13, 16. The number of correct digits roughly doubles each step.
Bisection on [1, 10] needs about 50 steps for the same accuracy.


This is the quadratic convergence promised in Convergence and cost, now on a real problem. The first step is a long jump with no correct digits; once close, the digit count doubles: 2, 6, 13, then all of them. Step 5 hits the reference value exactly, to the last bit. Of course in practice we do not know c50; the next slide shows how to stop without it.

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
A reusable Newton function
newton <- function(f, df, x0, tol = 1e-12, maxit = 50) {
  x <- x0
  for (k in 1:maxit) {
    step <- f(x) / df(x)
    x <- x - step
    if (abs(step) <= tol * abs(x)) return(list(root = x, iter = k))
  }
  warning("no convergence after ", maxit, " steps")
  list(root = x, iter = maxit)
}
newton(f, df, x0 = 1)$root        # 5 iterations
# [1] 3.261305

Stop when the step is small relative to x. Near a root the step is a good estimate of the error, because the next step is much smaller.
Cap the number of steps and warn, never fail silently.
Check afterwards: is |f(\text{root})| small, and is the root in the range that makes biological sense (c > 0)?


Ten lines, the hand-written version the design principles ask for. The stopping rule uses the size of the last step: with quadratic convergence the error after the step is far smaller than the step, so |step| is a slightly pessimistic estimate of the error before the step. A relative tolerance makes the rule work for doses in nM and in mM alike; tol = 1e-12 asks for about 12 digits. (For a root at exactly 0 a relative test never succeeds; add an absolute tolerance in that case.) maxit and the warning are the safety net for the failures later in the lecture. The post-checks are cheap and catch most of them.

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
Why digits double
Write e_k = x_k - x^*. Taylor to second order around x_k, then one line of algebra:
e_{k+1} \approx \frac{f''(x^*)}{2 f'(x^*)}\; e_k^2
Check on our run (error ratio e_{k+1}/e_k^2):










k

and |f''(c_{50}) / (2 f'(c_{50}))| = 0.0374. Squaring the error doubles the digits; the constant only shifts them a little.

Another view: Newton is fixed-point iteration with g(x) = x - f(x)/f'(x), and g'(x^*) = 0, the best possible case of |g'(x^*)| < 1.


The derivation: 0 = f(x) = f(x_k) - f’(x_k) e_k + f’‘/2 e_k^2 + …, divide by f’(x_k) and use the Newton update; the first-order terms cancel and what is left is the e_k^2 term. We do not do this in full on the slide; the exercise has a guided version. The table is the experimental check: the ratio settles at 0.037, which matches f’‘/(2f’) computed at the root (with numDeriv). The constant tells you what can spoil quadratic convergence: f’ = 0 at the root (a double root, the quiz) or a huge f’‘. The fixed-point view links back to the previous unit: g’(x) = 0 means the error is not shrunk by a constant factor but squared.

title: Newton and secant methods
section: Second biology problem: a rate from truncated counts
text:
Second biology problem: a rate from truncated counts
A gene’s UMI counts, recorded only in the 100 cells where it was detected (count ≥ 1):



count
1
2
3
4
5




cells
52
30
12
5
1



Model: Poisson with rate \lambda, zero-truncated (zeros are not seen). Log-likelihood and its derivative, the score:
\ell(\lambda) = \textstyle\sum_i x_i \log\lambda - n\lambda - n\log(1 - e^{-\lambda}) + \text{const}, \qquad S(\lambda) = \ell'(\lambda) = \frac{\sum_i x_i}{\lambda} - \frac{n}{1 - e^{-\lambda}}

The MLE \hat\lambda solves S(\lambda) = 0, i.e. \bar x = \lambda / (1 - e^{-\lambda}). No closed form.
The naive mean \bar x = 1.73 overestimates \lambda, because the zeros were thrown away.


Zero-truncated data are common in biology: counts recorded only where something was seen (UMIs in cells where a gene is detected, eggs in nests that have at least one, number of infected cells per infected well). For a plain Poisson the score is sum(x)/lambda - n and the MLE is the mean. The truncation adds the log(1 - e^-lambda) term, and the equation for the MLE becomes transcendental. Every maximum-likelihood fit you have run (glm, fitdistr, nls with likelihoods) solves an equation score = 0 like this one, usually with Newton or a relative of it. The maximisation view comes back in Part 9 (Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton).

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
Newton on the score
x <- rep(1:5, times = c(52, 30, 12, 5, 1))   # UMI counts, cells with >= 1 UMI
n <- length(x); sx <- sum(x)
S  <- function(l) sx / l - n / (-expm1(-l))        # score; -expm1(-l) = 1 - exp(-l)
dS <- function(l) -sx / l^2 + n * exp(-l) / expm1(-l)^2
fit <- newton(S, dS, x0 = mean(x))
fit$root; fit$iter
# [1] 1.21847
# [1] 6
1 / sqrt(-dS(fit$root))                           # standard error of lambda-hat
# [1] 0.1325479

\hat\lambda = 1.218, not 1.73. Starting at \bar x (a sensible guess from the data) converges in 6 steps.
-S'(\hat\lambda) is the observed information; 1/\sqrt{-S'(\hat\lambda)} is the usual standard error. Newton computes it for free.
expm1 from How computers store numbers keeps 1 - e^{-\lambda} accurate for small \lambda.


The same ten-line newton function, now on a statistical problem. S’ is the second derivative of the log-likelihood; minus it is the observed Fisher information, so the standard error comes out of the last Newton step at no cost. That is why Newton-type methods are standard in likelihood fitting (glm’s iteratively reweighted least squares is Fisher scoring, a Newton variant). Uncertainty of fitted parameters gets its own unit in Part 9 (Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters). expm1 matters for rates near 0, where 1 - exp(-l) cancels.

title: Newton and secant methods
section: The secant method: no derivative needed
text:
The secant method: no derivative needed
Often f' is tedious or impossible to write down (an ODE solution, a simulation). Replace the tangent by the line through the last two points:
x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)\,\frac{x_k - x_{k-1}}{f(x_k) - f(x_{k-1})}

The fraction is 1/\text{slope} of the chord, an estimate of 1/f'(x_k).
One new function evaluation per step (f(x_k); f(x_{k-1}) is reused). Newton needs two (f and f').
Needs two starting values. Unlike bisection, they need not bracket the root.


Point back to the right panel of the tangent picture. The secant method is Newton with the derivative replaced by a finite difference that uses points we already have, so it is free. The two start points do not need opposite signs; this is not regula falsi (false position), which keeps a bracket. In practice derivatives are often unavailable: if f involves solving an ODE or running a simulation, a hand-derived f’ does not exist.

Order p: e_{k+1} \approx C e_k^p. Bisection p = 1, secant p = 1.618 (the golden ratio), Newton p = 2.
Per function evaluation, secant (1.62) beats Newton (\sqrt2 = 1.41): two secant steps cost as much as one Newton step.


Digits = -log10(relative error). Bisection’s midpoint error wobbles (step 2 is a lucky hit), but its bound halves every step; it ends at about 12 digits after 40 steps. The secant digit counts grow by a factor of about 1.6 per step: 3.2, 5.3, 9.4, 15.6. Newton’s double. The flat part at the bottom is machine precision, eps times c50. The per-evaluation comparison: two Newton evaluations multiply the order by 2, so per evaluation the order is sqrt(2); a secant evaluation multiplies by 1.618. When f’ costs as much as f, the secant method is usually faster in time. Estimating p from three consecutive errors is in the exercise.

title: Newton and secant methods
section: Failure 1: a flat tangent throws you far away
text:
Failure 1: a flat tangent throws you far away




r <- newton(f, df, x0 = 10)$root
r
# [1] -3.04997
f(r)
# [1] 0             # a root!


At c_0 = 10 the curve is nearly flat (f' = 0.023), so f/f' is a huge step, to c_1 = -5.73.
Newton then converges, quickly and quietly, to an exact root at a negative dose. No warning.
Check: is the root in the meaningful range? Plot f. Start inside a bracket.


The formula for R accepts negative c, and it happens to have another root there. Newton does not know that doses are positive. This is the “confident wrong answer” of the introduction: converged, f is exactly zero in floating point, and biologically meaningless. Whenever f’ is small compared with f, the step f/f’ is large; near a plateau of a saturating curve that is always the case. The checks: look at the answer (negative dose), plot f over the plausible range, and start from a point inside a bracket where f changes sign. Solving in log dose would make negative doses impossible, but has its own failure (two slides on).

title: Newton and secant methods
section: Failure 2: a bad start for the MLE
text:
Failure 2: a bad start for the MLE




l <- 3                       # start
for (k in 1:6) {
  l <- l - S(l) / dS(l)
  cat(signif(l, 4), "")
}
# -0.4704 -1.066 -2.587
# -6.032 -12.33 -24.67


The score is convex and flattens for large \lambda; from \lambda_0 = 3 the tangent crosses zero at \lambda_1 = -0.47. From there Newton runs off to -\infty.
Starts up to about 2.7 converge; from 2.8 on they do not. The start must be close enough.
Check: \lambda > 0 at every step; the log-likelihood should increase at every step.


Newton converges only from close enough. “Close enough” is not a fixed distance; it depends on the shape of f. For large lambda the score behaves like sum(x)/lambda - n, and Newton on 1/lambda type functions overshoots badly: the exercise derives that the iteration for 1/x - a only converges from 0 < x0 < 2/a. Here that predicts trouble from about 2 x-bar = 3.5; the true limit is between 2.7 and 2.8. A good start (the mean, a method-of-moments estimate) avoids it, and so does a bracket. Optimisation routines check that each step increases the log-likelihood and shorten the step if not (line search, Part 9).

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
Failure 3: cycling forever




Michaelis–Menten, in log substrate u = \ln(S/K_m): solve v/V_{\max} = 0.5 (root S = K_m). Newton’s step is u_{k+1} = u_k - \sinh u_k.
u <- 2.1773189849653  # S0 = 8.82 Km
for (k in 1:6) {
  u <- u - sinh(u); cat(signif(u, 4), "")
}
# -2.177 2.177 -2.177 2.177 -2.177 2.177


Start at 8.82\,K_m: the tangents bounce between 8.82\,K_m and K_m/8.82 forever. Start at 10\,K_m: u grows, Inf, then NaN. Start at 5\,K_m: converges.
Check: cap the number of steps (maxit) and look at the last few iterates.


Working in log dose is good practice (doses are positive, curves are symmetric), but Newton can still fail on a sigmoid. For the logistic curve in u the Newton step simplifies to u - sinh(u) (exercise). A 2-cycle needs u - sinh(u) = -u, i.e. sinh(u) = 2u, at u = 2.177, S = 8.82 Km. Beyond it Newton diverges (u = 2.3 gives -2.64, 4.31, -33, 1e14, -Inf, NaN), inside it converges. Exact cycles are rare, but near-cycles that wander for many steps before escaping are common. The maxit cap plus a warning is what turns an endless loop into a message.

title: Newton and secant methods
section: Failures and checks at a glance
text:
Failures and checks at a glance








What goes wrong
Symptom
Check / fix




Start far from root, f' small
huge first step
plot f; start inside a bracket


Converges to the wrong root
root outside the meaningful range
check sign and range of the answer


Divergence
iterates grow, Inf, NaN
is.finite() on each iterate; maxit


Cycling
iterates repeat
maxit plus warning; print the last iterates


Wrong derivative
slow (linear) or no convergence
compare df with a finite difference


f'(x^*) = 0 (double root)
linear convergence, few digits
look at the digits-per-step


Secant: f(x_k) = f(x_{k-1})
division by 0
test before dividing



The cure for most of them: never leave a bracket.

A summary table to keep. Most of these failures share one cause: Newton and secant only use local information, so nothing stops them from leaving the region where the root is. If we know an interval with a sign change, we can refuse any step that leaves it. That is the idea of safeguarded methods, next. The double-root case is in the quiz: a tangency, e.g. at a saddle-node bifurcation, where f touches zero without crossing it; bracketing does not help there either, because there is no sign change.

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
Safeguarding: Brent’s method
Keep a bracket [a, b] with a sign change, and try a fast step:

Propose a fast step: secant, or inverse quadratic interpolation (a parabola x(f) through the last three points, evaluated at f = 0).
If the proposal falls outside the bracket, or the bracket has not shrunk enough lately, take a bisection step instead.
Evaluate f at the new point and keep the half that still has the sign change.


Guaranteed to converge, like bisection: never worse than about bisection’s pace.
Superlinear (order up to ~1.8) once close, like secant. No derivative needed.
This is R’s uniroot and Python’s scipy.optimize.brentq.


Brent (1973), building on Dekker. The details of when to switch are fiddly, but the idea fits on a slide: a fast method on a leash. Inverse quadratic interpolation fits x as a quadratic function of f through three points and reads off x at f = 0; it converges with order about 1.84. The bisection fallback guarantees that the bracket keeps shrinking, so the method cannot diverge, cycle or leave the interval. We do not implement Brent; we use it, and the exercise compares its function-evaluation count with ours.

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
uniroot in practice
r <- uniroot(f, interval = c(0.01, 100))
c(root = r$root, iter = r$iter, estim.prec = r$estim.prec)
#         root         iter   estim.prec
# 3.261305e+00 9.000000e+00 6.103516e-05
r$root - c50
# [1] -1.360226e-07                            # only ~7 digits!
r <- uniroot(f, interval = c(0.01, 100), tol = 1e-12)
r$root - c50; r$iter
# [1] 4.440892e-16
# [1] 10
uniroot(f, c(5, 100))          # Error: f() values at end points not of opposite sign

The default tol is \varepsilon^{1/4} \approx 1.2\times10^{-4}, an absolute tolerance: set tol yourself.
It needs a sign change; extendInt = "yes" widens a bad interval for you.


Three practical points. First, uniroot’s default tolerance is loose: fine for an EC50 reported to 3 digits, not fine if the root feeds into further computation (e.g. a derivative by finite differences, or an outer optimisation). estim.prec reports the achieved bracket width. Second, with a sensible tol it reaches machine precision in 10 iterations from a 10 000-fold wide bracket; bisection would need 50. Third, it refuses intervals without a sign change, which is exactly the safety we wanted. brentq in scipy has a tighter default (xtol = 2e-12, plus a relative rtol), but the same idea.

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
Back to the MLE, safely
uniroot(S, interval = c(0.01, 10), tol = 1e-10)$root
# [1] 1.21847
S(c(0.01, 10))
# [1] 7249.91667  -82.70454

A wide bracket of plausible rates is easy to give: S > 0 for small \lambda, S < 0 for large \lambda.
No start value to choose, no derivative, no run-off to negative rates.
When you need the derivative anyway (standard error), polish with one or two Newton steps from the bracketed answer.

Rule of thumb: bracket first (uniroot, brentq), use hand-written Newton when you need speed in a loop over thousands of genes, and then with a good start and checks.

The bracket [0.01, 10] covers any plausible rate for these data. uniroot finds the same 1.21847 that Newton found from the mean, and cannot fail the way Newton did from 3. In practice: for one-off roots, use uniroot with tol set. For a root inside a loop over 20 000 genes, Newton from a good start (the mean) converges in a handful of steps and is cheaper; add a fallback to uniroot for the genes where the checks fail.

title: Newton and secant methods
section: Checklist: before you trust a root
text:
Checklist: before you trust a root

Plot f over the plausible range. How many roots? Where?
Bracket the root if you can, and use a bracketing method (uniroot, brentq).
Set the tolerance yourself; know whether it is absolute or relative.
Check the answer: |f(x)| small, x in the meaningful range (positive dose, positive rate).
Hand-written Newton: check df against a finite difference; cap the iterations; warn on failure.
Look at the convergence: digits should double (Newton) or grow by ~1.6× (secant). If they grow by a fixed amount per step, something is wrong (derivative, double root).


Read through it once. The last point is the diagnostic that comes from this lecture: the digits-per-step table is not just a picture of the theory, it is a debugging tool. Linear convergence from a method that should be quadratic almost always means a wrong derivative or a root where f’ = 0.

title: Newton and secant methods
text:
Summary

Newton: x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)/f'(x_k), from the tangent line (first-order Taylor). Near a simple root, quadratic: e_{k+1} \approx \frac{f''}{2f'}\,e_k^2, digits double each step.
Secant: the tangent replaced by the chord through the last two points. No derivative, one evaluation per step, order 1.618.
Both converge only from close enough. Failures: a flat derivative sends the iterate far away (negative dose), a bad start diverges (negative rate), some starts cycle. Detect with range checks, is.finite(), maxit, and a plot of f.
Brent’s method (uniroot, brentq) keeps a sign-change bracket and uses fast steps inside it: guaranteed and fast. Set tol yourself.
Biology: an EC50 of a two-site curve and a maximum-likelihood rate are both roots with no closed form; the observed information -S'(\hat\lambda) from Newton gives the standard error.

Next: Newton for systems of equations, where f' becomes the Jacobian matrix and each step is a linear solve.

Recap the two methods, the convergence orders and the failure modes with their checks. Next unit: two or more unknowns (steady states of a toggle switch); Newton generalises directly, with the derivative replaced by the matrix of partial derivatives. The secant idea generalises too (Broyden, and later quasi-Newton optimisation in Part 9).

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
About this lecture
So far we solved one equation in one unknown. Biology rarely stops there: two genes regulate each other, so their steady state is two equations in two unknowns, solved together.

Partial derivatives: the slope in one direction while the other variables are held fixed. New for most of you; we go slowly, with numbers.
The Jacobian: all partial derivatives in one matrix. It plays the role of f'(x).
Newton for systems: linearise, then do one linear solve per step, solve(J, -F). Still quadratic convergence.
A finite-difference Jacobian when you cannot (or do not want to) differentiate by hand, and the library routine rootSolve::multiroot.
Biology: the genetic toggle switch. It has three steady states (bistability), and which one Newton finds depends on where it starts.


This unit closes Part 2. It reuses the one-variable Newton method from the previous unit and the ideas of quadratic convergence and the sqrt(eps) step from Convergence and cost. The genuinely new mathematics is the partial derivative and the Jacobian matrix. Audience survey says most students have never seen multivariate calculus, so the first third of the lecture is a slow introduction with numbers on every slide. The Jacobian comes back in Equilibria, stability and the phase plane (stability) and in Part 9 (optimisation), so time spent here pays off later.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: A biology problem: the toggle switch
text:
A biology problem: the toggle switch

Two genes whose proteins repress each other (Gardner, Cantor & Collins, Nature 2000). Concentrations u, v (in units of the repression threshold), time in units of the protein lifetime:
\frac{du}{dt} = \frac{\alpha}{1 + v^{n}} - u, \qquad \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{\alpha}{1 + u^{n}} - v, \qquad \alpha = 3,\; n = 2

First term: production, a Hill function that falls as the repressor rises. Second term: degradation and dilution.
\alpha = promoter strength, n = Hill coefficient (cooperativity).


The synthetic toggle switch was one of the two founding papers of synthetic biology (together with the repressilator, same issue of Nature). Real version: LacI and TetR in E. coli. The same motif appears in natural cell-fate decisions, for example GATA1 and PU.1 in blood cell differentiation. The model is dimensionless: concentrations are measured in units of the repressor concentration that halves expression, time in units of the protein lifetime. With alpha = 3 the maximal production is three times the repression threshold. We use alpha = 3 and n = 2 throughout; the phase-plane unit reuses exactly this model.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Steady states: two equations, two unknowns
text:
Steady states: two equations, two unknowns




A steady state has du/dt = 0 and dv/dt = 0:
\begin{aligned}
F_1(u, v) &= \frac{3}{1 + v^2} - u = 0\\[2pt]
F_2(u, v) &= \frac{3}{1 + u^2} - v = 0
\end{aligned}

Each equation alone is a curve. Steady states are where the curves cross.
Here: three crossings. Two “decided” states (U on/V off, V on/U off) and one in between.
Two stable states = bistability: a memory switch.



Write the system as a vector function F of a vector x = (u, v); a steady state is a root, F(x) = 0. The blue curve is where u is not changing, the red where v is not changing (these curves are called nullclines; the phase-plane unit uses them more). Point at the three crossings. The cell sits in one of the two outer states and stays there: that is cellular memory. Which state is reached depends on history. The middle one exists, but (as we will see in the phase-plane unit) it is unstable. Our job today: compute these points to 15 digits, for this model and for models with many genes where no picture is possible.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Why a new method?
alpha <- 3; n <- 2
F <- function(x) {
  u <- x[1]; v <- x[2]
  c(alpha / (1 + v^n) - u,
    alpha / (1 + u^n) - v)
}
F(c(2.618, 0.382))          # close to the "U on" state?
# [1] -2.533501e-05 -2.533358e-05
F(c(1, 1))
# [1] 0.5 0.5

With 2 genes we could substitute one equation into the other and use a 1-D method. With 20 genes we cannot.
We could simulate the ODE until it stops moving. That is slow near a steady state, and it never finds the unstable middle one.
Newton generalises directly: one method for any number of equations.


F takes a vector of length 2 and returns a vector of length 2. A root makes both entries zero at once. The first test point is close to a root: both residuals are about 2.5e-5. Substitution: v = 3/(1+u^2), plug into the first equation, get one equation in u, use uniroot. Fine for two genes, impossible to organise for a network of twenty. Simulation: the approach to a steady state is exponential with a rate set by the slowest decay, so getting 12 digits can take a long simulation, and an unstable state is never reached by simulation. Newton handles all of that, and we can check it costs only a handful of steps.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Recap: Newton in one variable
Replace f by its tangent line at x_k and solve the line instead:
f(x_k + \delta) \approx f(x_k) + f'(x_k)\,\delta = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \delta = -\frac{f(x_k)}{f'(x_k)}, \qquad x_{k+1} = x_k + \delta
Example from Newton and secant methods: f(x) = x^2 - 2, x_0 = 1:

To do the same for \mathbf F(u, v) we need the “derivative” of a function of two variables that returns two numbers.

One-slide recap only; the previous unit has the details (derivation, failure modes, the secant method). The key idea to carry over: approximate the nonlinear function by a linear one, solve the linear problem exactly, repeat. Digits roughly double each step: quadratic convergence. For a system, “linear function” will mean a matrix times a vector, and “solve the linear problem” will mean solving a linear system. The missing piece is the derivative.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Partial derivatives: hold the others fixed
text:
Partial derivatives: hold the others fixed
F_1(u, v) = \dfrac{3}{1+v^2} - u depends on two numbers. Ask one question at a time:

How fast does F_1 change when only u moves? Treat v as a constant and differentiate in u as usual: \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial u} = -1
How fast does F_1 change when only v moves? Treat u as a constant (it drops out) and use the chain rule on 3(1+v^2)^{-1}: \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial v} = -\frac{3 \cdot 2v}{(1+v^2)^2} = -\frac{6v}{(1+v^2)^2}
At the point (u, v) = (3, 0.5): \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial v} = -\dfrac{6 \cdot 0.5}{1.25^2} = -\dfrac{3}{1.5625} = -1.92.

The curly \partial (“partial”) just means: other variables held fixed.

Go slowly; this is the first time many students see this. A partial derivative is nothing new: it is the ordinary derivative of a one-variable function, obtained by freezing all the other variables at numbers. Freeze v at 0.5 and F1 is 2.4 - u, a straight line with slope -1. Freeze u at 3 and F1 is 3/(1+v^2) - 3, a curve in v whose slope at v = 0.5 is -1.92. Read the units: dF1/dv = -1.92 means that raising the repressor V by 0.01 lowers F1 (the net rate of change of U) by about 0.0192. Work the chain rule on the board: d/dv (1+v2)-1 = -(1+v2)-2 * 2v.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Partial derivatives are slopes of slices
text:
Partial derivatives are slopes of slices

f1 <- function(u, v) alpha / (1 + v^2) - u
h <- 1e-6
(f1(3 + h, 0.5) - f1(3, 0.5)) / h      # move u only
# [1] -1
(f1(3, 0.5 + h) - f1(3, 0.5)) / h      # move v only
# [1] -1.92

Left: freeze v = 0.5 and plot F1 against u: a straight line, slope -1 everywhere. Right: freeze u = 3 and plot F1 against v: a curve, and the dashed tangent at v = 0.5 has slope -1.92. The code checks both numbers with a forward difference, exactly as in Convergence and cost: nudge one input, keep the other fixed, divide the change by the nudge. This is also the recipe for the finite-difference Jacobian later in the lecture. If a hand-derived partial derivative disagrees with this check in the first few digits, the hand derivation is wrong.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: The Jacobian: all partial derivatives in one matrix
text:
The Jacobian: all partial derivatives in one matrix
Row i = equation F_i, column j = variable x_j:


J = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial v} \\[8pt] \dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial v}\end{pmatrix}
\phantom{J} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -\dfrac{6v}{(1+v^2)^2} \\[8pt] -\dfrac{6u}{(1+u^2)^2} & -1\end{pmatrix}
At (3, 0.5): \dfrac{6\cdot 3}{(1+9)^2} = 0.18 and \dfrac{6\cdot0.5}{1.25^2} = 1.92.

J <- function(x) {
  u <- x[1]; v <- x[2]
  matrix(c(-1, -alpha * n * v^(n - 1) / (1 + v^n)^2,
           -alpha * n * u^(n - 1) / (1 + u^n)^2, -1),
         nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
}
J(c(3, 0.5))
#       [,1]  [,2]
# [1,] -1.00 -1.92
# [2,] -0.18 -1.00


The Jacobian (after Carl Jacobi) is the multivariable version of f’(x). For n equations in n unknowns it is an n by n matrix. Check the bottom-left entry by hand: 6 * 3 / (1 + 9)^2 = 18/100 = 0.18. Read the matrix as biology: the diagonal -1 is degradation (each protein reduces its own rate of change); the off-diagonal entries are the repression strengths, how much each protein lowers the production of the other. At (3, 0.5), V at 0.5 is right on the steep part of its Hill curve, so it acts strongly on U (-1.92); U at 3 is far above threshold, the Hill curve is flat there, so a small change in U hardly matters to V (-0.18). byrow = TRUE lets us type the matrix row by row as it is printed.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
The linear approximation, with numbers
One variable: f(x + \delta) \approx f(x) + f'(x)\,\delta. Two variables, one line per equation:
\begin{aligned}
F_1(u + \delta_u, v + \delta_v) &\approx F_1 + \tfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial u}\delta_u + \tfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial v}\delta_v\\
F_2(u + \delta_u, v + \delta_v) &\approx F_2 + \tfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial u}\delta_u + \tfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial v}\delta_v
\end{aligned}
In matrix form: \mathbf F(\mathbf x + \boldsymbol\delta) \approx \mathbf F(\mathbf x) + J\,\boldsymbol\delta (matrix J times vector \boldsymbol\delta).
x <- c(3, 0.5); d <- c(-0.1, 0.05)
F(x + d)                       # the true value
# [1] -0.5967370 -0.2311902
F(x) + J(x) %*% d              # the linear prediction
#        [,1]
# [1,] -0.596
# [2,] -0.232

Each change adds up: moving u changes F1 by (dF1/du) times the move, moving v changes it by (dF1/dv) times its move, and for small moves the two effects simply add. Written as a matrix-vector product that is J times delta. Check one entry by hand: F1 = -0.6, plus (-1)(-0.1) = +0.1, plus (-1.92)(0.05) = -0.096, total -0.596. True value -0.5967: agreement to 3 digits for a step of size 0.1; the mismatch is second order in delta, just as for the tangent line. %*% is R’s matrix product (Python: @).

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: The Newton step: one linear solve
text:
The Newton step: one linear solve
Ask for \mathbf F(\mathbf x_k + \boldsymbol\delta) = \mathbf 0 in the linear approximation:
\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k) + J(\mathbf x_k)\,\boldsymbol\delta = \mathbf 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \boxed{J(\mathbf x_k)\,\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k)}, \qquad \mathbf x_{k+1} = \mathbf x_k + \boldsymbol\delta







one variable
system




f(x_k), a number
\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k), a vector


f'(x_k), a number
J(\mathbf x_k), a matrix


\delta = -f/f' (divide)
solve J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F (linear system)


fails if f' = 0
fails if J is singular (\det J = 0)




Each step is a linear system, which we know how to solve (Gaussian elimination). In R: solve(J, -F).


This slide is the whole method. Division by the derivative becomes solving a linear system with the Jacobian. Write the analogy table on the board. “Singular” is the matrix version of “derivative zero”: the linear approximation then has no unique solution, and near-singular Jacobians give huge steps, just as a nearly flat tangent does in one dimension. We will see that failure later in the lecture.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
One step by hand
Start \mathbf x_0 = (3, 0.5). We have \mathbf F(\mathbf x_0) = (-0.6, -0.2) and J from before. Solve
\begin{pmatrix} -1 & -1.92 \\ -0.18 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\delta_u\\ \delta_v\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.2 \end{pmatrix}

Row 2 minus 0.18\times row 1: (-1 + 0.3456)\,\delta_v = 0.2 - 0.108, so \delta_v = 0.092 / (-0.6544) = -0.1406.
Row 1: -\delta_u = 0.6 + 1.92\,\delta_v = 0.3301, so \delta_u = -0.3301.
\mathbf x_1 = (3 - 0.3301,\; 0.5 - 0.1406) = (2.6699,\; 0.3594).

delta <- solve(J(c(3, 0.5)), -F(c(3, 0.5)))
delta
# [1] -0.3300733 -0.1405868
F(c(3, 0.5) + delta)              # residual: was (-0.6, -0.2)
# [1] -0.013126396  0.009658204

Gaussian elimination on a 2 by 2 system, as in a first linear algebra course. The residual went from size 0.6 to size 0.013 in one step. The exact steady state is (2.6180, 0.3820), so the error went from 0.4 to 0.05. Students repeat this by hand in the exercise and do a second step. Note: never compute the inverse matrix; solve(J, b) solves the system directly. Why that matters is a topic of Gaussian elimination as LU.

title: Newton for systems of equations
Newton for systems of equations
Newton for systems of equations
section: Three steady states: which one do we get?
text:
Three steady states: which one do we get?
starts <- rbind(c(3, 0.5), c(0.5, 3), c(1, 1), c(1, 0.2), c(4, 4))
t(apply(starts, 1, function(s) newton_sys(F, J, s)))   # (printing switched off)
#          [,1]     [,2]
# [1,] 2.618034 0.381966       U on, V off
# [2,] 0.381966 2.618034       V on, U off
# [3,] 1.213412 1.213412       middle
# [4,] 0.381966 2.618034       V on: although U > V at the start!
# [5,] 1.213412 1.213412       middle

Bistable: two “decided” states, plus the middle one. Newton finds one root per start.
To find them all: run from many starts and collect the distinct answers.
The start (1, 0.2) has more U than V, yet Newton lands on “V on”. Newton’s choice is not the cell’s choice.


The apply line runs Newton from each row of starts (the cat line is switched off for this slide). The first two answers are mirror images: the model is symmetric under swapping u and v. The middle state has u = v = 1.2134, the real root of u^3 + u - 3 = 0. A start on the diagonal u = v stays on the diagonal for ever (by symmetry), so (1,1) and (4,4) can only find the middle state. The fourth start is the interesting one: biologically a cell with U = 1 and V = 0.2 will switch U on, but Newton jumps to the other state. Next slide shows why.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Where Newton goes vs where the cell goes
text:
Where Newton goes vs where the cell goes


Left: colour = the steady state Newton converges to from that start. Right: where the ODE (the cell) ends up.
Newton’s regions (basins) are curved, with thin bands of all colours; the middle, unstable state takes 57 % of this square.


Each pixel is a start (u0, v0); colour = the root reached. Right panel: simulate the ODE from the same start; the line u = v separates the two fates (by symmetry), and nobody ever ends in the middle state because it is unstable: the slightest push sends the cell to one side. Left panel: Newton’s basins have nothing to do with that. Newton is a root finder: it finds points where F = 0, stable or unstable, and the middle state, with 57 percent of the square, is the most common answer. Near the boundaries, thin interleaved bands appear, where tiny changes of the start change the answer. Lesson: Newton tells you where the steady states are, not which one the cell goes to, nor whether a steady state is stable. Stability needs the eigenvalues of the Jacobian: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Bistability needs a strong promoter




Run Newton from a 7 × 7 grid of starts for each promoter strength \alpha, keep the distinct roots.

\alpha < 2: one steady state; the circuit is not a switch.
\alpha > 2: three; the circuit is bistable.
Designing the switch (Gardner et al.) meant tuning promoters until the circuit was in the bistable range.



This is the biological payoff: the number of steady states is a property you can compute, and it decides whether the circuit works as a memory. Gardner and colleagues showed exactly this kind of diagram for their toggle and picked promoters and ribosome binding sites to sit inside the bistable region. For this symmetric model with n = 2 the threshold is exactly alpha = 2 (the exercise shows why: the outer states satisfy u + v = alpha, uv = 1, which has real solutions only for alpha >= 2). With n = 1 (no cooperativity) there is never bistability. The multi-start loop is the honest way to count roots when you do not have a formula, and it can miss roots whose basins your starts do not touch.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: No formula for J? Finite differences
text:
No formula for J? Finite differences
Often \mathbf F is a long function (a 20-gene network, a model with many terms) and deriving J by hand is tedious and error-prone. Approximate column j by nudging only x_j:
J_{:,j} \approx \frac{\mathbf F(\mathbf x + h_j\,\mathbf e_j) - \mathbf F(\mathbf x)}{h_j}, \qquad h_j = \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\max(|x_j|, 1) \approx 1.5\times10^{-8}\max(|x_j|, 1)
(\mathbf e_j = 1 in place j, 0 elsewhere.)

One nudge gives a whole column: how every equation responds to x_j.
Cost: n + 1 evaluations of \mathbf F per Jacobian.
h = \sqrt\varepsilon balances truncation and rounding error (Convergence and cost): about 8 correct digits.


This is the forward difference from Convergence and cost, applied one variable at a time. Column j, not row: moving one input changes all outputs at once. Scaling h with the size of x_j keeps the nudge relative: a concentration of 1000 needs a bigger absolute nudge than one of 0.001. For n genes the Jacobian costs n + 1 function evaluations; for big models (or expensive F, like an ODE solve) this dominates, which is why library codes reuse a Jacobian over several steps (Broyden’s method, quasi-Newton in Part 9). Central differences give more digits for twice the cost; see Numerical differentiation.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Finite-difference Jacobian in R


fd_jacobian <- function(F, x,
                        h = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)) {
  Fx <- F(x)
  Jm <- matrix(0, length(Fx), length(x))
  for (j in seq_along(x)) {
    hj <- h * max(abs(x[j]), 1)
    xh <- x; xh[j] <- x[j] + hj
    Jm[, j] <- (F(xh) - Fx) / hj     # column j
  }
  Jm
}
max(abs(fd_jacobian(F, c(3, 0.5)) - J(c(3, 0.5))))
# [1] 1.311302e-08




Use it also to check a hand-derived J: a wrong entry shows up as an error much larger than 10^{-7}.


Twelve lines, and it works for any F of any size. The error 1.3e-8 is what sqrt(eps) predicts. The figure shows the same V as in Convergence and cost: truncation error on the right (slope 1), rounding error on the left (slope -1), best near h = 1.5e-8. Comparing a hand-written Jacobian with the finite-difference one is the standard bug check before trusting a Newton code: a sign error or a missing factor gives a difference of order 1, not 1e-8. numDeriv::jacobian in R does this with a more accurate (Richardson) scheme.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: The cost of a step: one linear solve
text:
The cost of a step: one linear solve
Per Newton step for n genes:







part
cost




evaluate \mathbf F
depends on the model, often \sim n


Jacobian by finite differences
n + 1 evaluations of \mathbf F


solve J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F (Gaussian elimination)
\approx \tfrac23 n^3 operations




n = 2: nothing. n = 1000: \approx 7\times10^8 per step, still under a second. n = 20\,000: hours, unless J is sparse (most genes do not regulate most others).
Never form solve(J) (the inverse) and multiply: solve(J, -F) is cheaper and more accurate.


For small networks the cost is irrelevant. For genome-scale models the linear solve dominates, and the structure of J matters: a gene regulatory network has few edges, so J is mostly zeros, and sparse solvers are vastly faster. The why and how of these costs (LU factorisation, why not the inverse, sparsity) is Part 3: Gaussian elimination as LU and Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse. Today: one step = one linear solve.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
The library routine: rootSolve::multiroot
library(rootSolve)
sol <- multiroot(f = F, start = c(3, 0.5))      # Jacobian by finite differences
sol$root;  sol$f.root;  sol$iter
# [1] 2.618034 0.381966
# [1] -1.471712e-12  8.891221e-13
# [1] 5
sol2 <- multiroot(f = F, start = c(3, 0.5), jacfunc = J)  # supply your own J

multiroot is Newton–Raphson with a finite-difference Jacobian (unless you pass jacfunc), plus tolerances (rtol, atol, ctol), an iteration limit and sparse-Jacobian options for large models.
It stops at its own tolerance: here \|\mathbf F\| \approx 10^{-12}, not 10^{-16}. Check f.root, and set atol tighter if you need it.
It finds one root, from your start. Multiple starts are still your job.


rootSolve was written for steady states of ODE models (it has runsteady and stode for that purpose too). The output list has root, f.root (the residual at the root), iter and estim.precis. Default tolerances are about 1e-8 absolute, so the answer is correct to about 12 digits here, which is plenty for biology but worth knowing. Python users: scipy.optimize.root (default method hybr, Powell’s hybrid method from MINPACK, which adds a trust region so that it cannot take arbitrarily large steps) or the older fsolve. Neither knows about multiple steady states.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Failure 1: a nearly singular Jacobian
x0 <- c(1.9, 0.5)
det(J(x0))                          # close to 0
# [1] -0.02992175
x0 + solve(J(x0), -F(x0))           # the first step
# [1] -5.136430  4.425224           # negative concentration!
newton_sys(F, J, c(1.9, 0.5))       # ends in the middle state
newton_sys(F, J, c(2.0, 0.55))      # a nearby start: "U on"

\det J \approx 0: the linear model is nearly flat in some direction, so the step is huge. It lands at u < 0, which is not a concentration.
With a non-integer Hill coefficient (n = 2.5) the same kind of jump gives (-3.2)^{2.5} = NaN, and Newton returns NaN.
Check: watch \|\boldsymbol\delta\| and \det J (or the condition number); check all(is.finite(x)) and all(x >= 0).


The analogue of a flat tangent in 1-D. Near the curve where det J = 0 (here det J = 1 - (dF1/dv)(dF2/du)), the Newton step blows up. This is where the thin coloured bands of the basin picture come from: start near det J = 0 and you are thrown far away, and from there you can end anywhere. Two starts 0.1 apart end in different steady states. Negative concentrations are a sign the iteration has left the biologically meaningful region; with v^2 it happens to recover, but with x^2.5 negative numbers give NaN. Remedies used by library codes: damping (take only part of the step if the residual does not decrease), trust regions (scipy’s hybr), or working with log-concentrations so that they stay positive. In rootSolve: multiroot(F, c(2, 0.5)) with n = 2.5 warns “steady-state not reached”; multiroot(F, c(2, 0.5), positive = TRUE) keeps the iterates non-negative and converges to (2.955, 0.187).

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Failure 2: a root, but not the one you wanted
text:
Failure 2: a root, but not the one you wanted

Newton from (1, 1), (2, 2) or (4, 4) converges, quickly and correctly, to the middle state (1.2134, 1.2134): a start with u = v stays on the diagonal by symmetry.
The residual is 10^{-16}: nothing in the output warns you that this state is unstable, i.e. that no real cell sits there.
A single run hides the other two states completely: you would conclude the switch is not bistable.

Checks

Run from many starts (a grid, or random) and list the distinct roots.
Check each root for stability: eigenvalues of J at the root (Equilibria, stability and the phase plane), or a short ODE simulation from a nearby point.


This failure is the worse one, because everything looks fine: quadratic convergence, residual at machine precision. In practice people start from a symmetric guess (all genes equal, all at 1) more often than you would think. The cure is not a better root finder but a better procedure: many starts, deduplicate, then classify each root. Here the middle state is a saddle: J there has eigenvalues 0.19 and -2.19, one positive. That calculation is the topic of the phase-plane unit.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Checklist for Newton on a system
text:
Checklist for Newton on a system

Check J against a finite-difference Jacobian before anything else (difference \sim 10^{-8}, not \sim 1).
Watch the iteration: \|\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k)\| should fall fast (digits double). If it grows or stalls, the start is too far or J is wrong.
Look at the root: finite, non-negative, residual small (f.root in multiroot).
Large steps / tiny \det J → the start is near a singular Jacobian; try another start or a damped/trust-region solver.
Many starts → collect distinct roots; one run finds one root.
Stability is a separate question: a root of \mathbf F is not necessarily where the cell goes.


A practical list to go through whenever a steady-state computation is part of an analysis. The first item catches most bugs in hand-written Newton codes. The last two items are about the biology: counting and classifying steady states.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Summary

A partial derivative \partial F_i/\partial x_j is an ordinary derivative with all other variables held fixed. The Jacobian J collects them: row = equation, column = variable.
Linearise: \mathbf F(\mathbf x + \boldsymbol\delta) \approx \mathbf F(\mathbf x) + J\boldsymbol\delta. Newton step: solve J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F, set \mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \boldsymbol\delta. One linear solve per step: solve(J(x), -F(x)).
Convergence is quadratic near a root, as in one variable.
Finite-difference Jacobian: one column per nudge, h = \sqrt\varepsilon\max(|x_j|, 1), about 8 correct digits, n + 1 evaluations of \mathbf F.
Library: rootSolve::multiroot (R), scipy.optimize.root (Python).
The toggle switch has three steady states when \alpha > 2 (bistable). Which one Newton finds depends on the start, in complicated ways, and it finds unstable states as happily as stable ones.
Failures: nearly singular J (huge steps, negative concentrations, NaN), and converging to a root you did not want. Checks: step size, positivity, many starts.

Next: Part 3, Gaussian elimination as LU: what solve does inside, and what it costs.

Recap the three new objects: partial derivative, Jacobian, Newton step as a linear solve. The toggle switch comes back in Equilibria, stability and the phase plane, where the Jacobian at each steady state decides its stability, and the Jacobian comes back in Part 9 as the derivative of a gradient (the Hessian) in Newton’s method for optimisation. Part 3 opens the black box solve.

title: Exercise: pivoting, norms and conditioning
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain why Gaussian elimination without pivoting fails on a tiny pivot, and show it with 3-digit arithmetic,
carry out partial pivoting by hand and write \(PA = LU\) for a \(3\times 3\) matrix,
compute the 1-, 2- and \(\infty\)-norms of a vector and the 1- and \(\infty\)-norms of a matrix,
compute the condition number \(\kappa(A)\) of a \(2\times2\) matrix by hand and with kappa() / np.linalg.cond / nalgebra’s singular_values(),
use the rule “lose about \(\log_{10}\kappa\) digits” for rounding errors and for measurement noise,
tell the residual from the error, and say what each one checks,
predict how much detector noise is amplified when unmixing dyes with overlapping spectra.

The by-hand part uses pen and paper (and a calculator for B1, where you must round to 3 digits on purpose). The code part checks the hand answers and then works at sizes where only code works.

text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:
