title: Numerical differentiation
text:
About this lecture
A derivative is a rate: how fast a culture grows, how fast a drug is cleared, how steeply a log-likelihood rises. A computer only has function values, so it estimates the rate from a few nearby values.

Stencils from Taylor: forward, backward and central differences, a one-sided formula for the ends of a data set, and the second derivative.
The best step for each: \varepsilon^{1/2}, \varepsilon^{1/3}, \varepsilon^{1/4}, and why.
Richardson extrapolation: combine two poor estimates into a good one (what numDeriv::grad does).
Measured data: differentiating amplifies noise. Widen the stencil or smooth first.
Gradients for fitting by finite differences, how they fail inside optim, and the alternatives: the complex step and automatic differentiation.

Biology: the instantaneous growth rate from a noisy plate-reader OD curve; the gradient of a log-likelihood when fitting the growth curve.

This unit opens Part 7. In Convergence and cost we used the forward difference of the logistic OD curve to see the truncation/rounding V and only previewed the central difference. Here we do the systematic version: where every stencil comes from, how to pick the step, how to do better than any single stencil, and what happens with real, noisy data. The second half is about gradients, the multivariate version, because that is where most biologists meet numerical derivatives without noticing: every optimiser that is not given a gradient computes one by finite differences.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Recap: the V from Convergence and cost
text:
Recap: the V from Convergence and cost
Logistic OD curve N(t) = \dfrac{K}{1 + (K/N_0 - 1)\,e^{-rt}}, K = 1.2, N_0 = 0.05, r = 0.8 per hour. True growth rate at t = 3 h: N'(3) = 0.21026 OD/h.

Forward difference \dfrac{N(t+h) - N(t)}{h}: truncation error \tfrac{h}{2}N'', order 1.
Rounding error \approx \varepsilon|N|/h: the two values agree in almost all digits, and dividing by a small h blows up their rounding.
Total error: a V on log–log axes, best h \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon} \approx 10^{-8}, best error \approx 10^{-8}: half the digits lost.
The central difference \dfrac{N(t+h) - N(t-h)}{2h} had slope 2 and a deeper V.
The ratio check \dfrac{D(h) - D(h/2)}{D(h/2) - D(h/4)} \approx 2^p tells truncation regime from rounding regime without the exact answer.

Today: where these formulas come from, how to build any formula you need, and what changes when N is measured, not computed.

One slide only: students who skipped Convergence and cost should go back to it. The three facts to carry forward: truncation error falls like h^p, rounding error grows like eps/h, and the best step balances them. Everything in the first half of this lecture is a variation on that balance. The second half replaces eps by the measurement noise, which is about 10^13 times larger.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: The problem: growth rate from a plate reader
text:
The problem: growth rate from a plate reader
A plate reader measures OD600 every 10 minutes for 10 hours (61 values, 3 decimals, noise sd \approx 0.005). We want the growth rate N'(t) and its maximum.

The curve looks clean. Its central differences do not: they jump by \pm 0.03, and one is negative, a culture “shrinking” in mid-growth.

Simulated data: the same logistic curve, plus Gaussian noise of sd 0.005 OD (a realistic plate-reader noise level), rounded to three decimals as a plate reader exports them. Left panel: you cannot see the noise by eye. Right panel: the naive derivative, (y[i+1] - y[i-1]) / (20 min), is visibly noisy, overshoots the maximum (0.27 instead of 0.24) and goes negative near the end. The maximum specific growth rate, the number many papers report, is read off exactly this kind of curve. By the end of the lecture we know why the noise grows when we differentiate and two ways to tame it. First, though, the stencils themselves.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Taylor, three times
Write the neighbours of t as Taylor series around t (prime = derivative at t):

\begin{aligned}
N(t+h) &= N + h N' + \tfrac{h^2}{2} N'' + \tfrac{h^3}{6} N''' + \tfrac{h^4}{24} N'''' + \dots \\
N(t-h) &= N - h N' + \tfrac{h^2}{2} N'' - \tfrac{h^3}{6} N''' + \tfrac{h^4}{24} N'''' - \dots \\
N(t+2h) &= N + 2h N' + \tfrac{4h^2}{2} N'' + \tfrac{8h^3}{6} N''' + \dots
\end{aligned}

For the OD curve at t = 3:



N
N'
N''
N'''
N''''




0.38879
0.21026
0.05921
-0.04227
-0.06170



Recipe: add multiples of these rows so that everything cancels except the derivative you want. What is left over is the error.

This is the only tool we need. Each row is the Taylor polynomial from first-year calculus, evaluated at a shifted point. The minus signs in the second row alternate because (-h)^k changes sign with k. The derivatives of the logistic come from differentiating N’ = r N (1 - N/K) repeatedly; students do not need to compute them, but having the numbers lets us check every error formula against the computer. Notation: N, N’, N’’ without an argument all mean “at t”.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Forward and backward differences
Forward: take row 1, subtract N, divide by h: \frac{N(t+h) - N(t)}{h} = N' + \underbrace{\tfrac{h}{2} N''}_{\text{error}} + O(h^2)
Backward: take row 2, the same way: \frac{N(t) - N(t-h)}{h} = N' - \tfrac{h}{2} N'' + O(h^2)

Both are first order. At t = 3: error \approx \pm 0.0296\,h; with h = 0.1 h, +0.0029 and -0.0030.
The errors have opposite signs: forward overestimates, backward underestimates (the curve bends upwards at t = 3).
Use: the backward difference needs only past values, the forward only future ones. At the last measurement of a time course, backward is all you have.


The leading error term is the first Taylor term we did not cancel. The O(h^2) collects the rest. For a curve that bends upwards (N’’ > 0), the forward secant is steeper than the tangent and the backward secant shallower. That the two errors are almost equal and opposite is the hint for the next slide: average them.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Central difference: let the errors cancel
text:
Central difference: let the errors cancel
Subtract row 2 from row 1: the even terms (N, N'', N'''') cancel. N(t+h) - N(t-h) = 2hN' + \tfrac{2h^3}{6} N''' + \dots
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{N(t+h) - N(t-h)}{2h} = N' + \underbrace{\tfrac{h^2}{6} N'''}_{\text{error}} + O(h^4)

Second order: halving h quarters the error. At t = 3: error \approx -0.00705\,h^2, so -7.0\times10^{-5} at h = 0.1, forty times smaller than forward.
Same cost as forward (two evaluations), if N(t) is not needed anyway.
It is the average of forward and backward; their \pm\tfrac{h}{2}N'' errors cancel.
It needs a point on each side: not available at the first and last time point.


Symmetry is what buys the extra order. Note the next error term is O(h^4), not O(h^3): only even powers of h appear in the central difference’s error. That fact is what makes Richardson extrapolation so effective later. One caveat about cost: if you need N(t) anyway (e.g. inside a Newton step), the forward difference costs one extra evaluation and the central two.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Any stencil you need: match Taylor terms
text:
Any stencil you need: match Taylor terms
At the first time point there is no t - h. Look for weights w_0, w_1, w_2 with w_0 N(t) + w_1 N(t+h) + w_2 N(t+2h) \approx h\,N'(t). Matching the N, hN' and h^2N'' terms of the Taylor rows gives a 3\times3 linear system:
s <- c(0, 1, 2)                            # offsets: t, t+h, t+2h
A <- outer(0:2, s, function(k, s) s^k / factorial(k))   # row k: Taylor term k
solve(A, c(0, 1, 0))                       # want: 0 N + 1 hN' + 0 h^2 N''
# [1] -1.5  2.0 -0.5
So N'(t) \approx \dfrac{-3N(t) + 4N(t+h) - N(t+2h)}{2h}, error -\tfrac{h^2}{3}N''': second order with one-sided data.

Same method with offsets (-1, 0, 1) and right-hand side (0, 0, 1) gives the second derivative.
np.gradient uses central differences inside and (with edge_order=2) this formula at the ends.


This is the method of undetermined coefficients. Row k of A holds s^k / k!, the Taylor coefficient of h^k N^(k) at offset s; the right-hand side says which derivative we want. Three points can match three terms, so the first unmatched term, k = 3, is the error. The linear system ties back to Part 3: it is a small Vandermonde-type matrix. More points give higher order: offsets -2..2 give the five-point formula (1, -8, 0, 8, -1)/12h with error O(h^4) (exercise C2). The same idea builds every stencil in the diffusion units.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
The second derivative
Add rows 1 and 2: now the odd terms cancel. N(t+h) + N(t-h) = 2N + h^2 N'' + \tfrac{2h^4}{24} N'''' + \dots
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\frac{N(t+h) - 2N(t) + N(t-h)}{h^2} = N'' + \underbrace{\tfrac{h^2}{12} N''''}_{\text{error}} + \dots

Second order. At t = 3: error \approx -0.00514\,h^2.
Biology: N'' is the acceleration of growth. It changes sign at the inflection point, the time of fastest growth (t = 3.92 h here).
This (1, -2, 1)/h^2 stencil is the workhorse of Part 10: in space it becomes the diffusion term D\,\partial^2 c/\partial x^2, in The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences.



The picture summarises the four stencils so far: dots are the points used, numbers the weights, right column the divisor. Filled dots only. For the second derivative the weights must sum to zero (a constant has no curvature) and the stencil is symmetric. Flag the forward reference clearly: the diffusion equation replaces t by a space coordinate x, and the second difference of concentrations on a grid of channels is exactly this formula. Its error, h^2/12 times the fourth derivative, is the spatial accuracy of every scheme in Part 10.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
All four in R
K <- 1.2; N0 <- 0.05; r <- 0.8
od <- function(t) K / (1 + (K / N0 - 1) * exp(-r * t))
gr <- function(t) r * od(t) * (1 - od(t) / K)            # exact N'(t)
t0 <- 3; exact <- gr(t0); d2 <- r * exact * (1 - 2 * od(t0) / K)  # N'(3), N''(3)
h   <- c(0.1, 0.05, 0.025)
fwd <- (od(t0 + h) - od(t0)) / h
bwd <- (od(t0) - od(t0 - h)) / h
cen <- (od(t0 + h) - od(t0 - h)) / (2 * h)
sec <- (od(t0 + h) - 2 * od(t0) + od(t0 - h)) / h^2
err <- cbind(fwd = fwd - exact, bwd = bwd - exact, cen = cen - exact, sec = sec - d2)
err[1, ] / err[2, ]                                      # halve h: error ratio
#      fwd      bwd      cen      sec
# 1.974603 2.022227 3.999432 3.997985

Ratios \approx 2 (first order) and \approx 4 (second order), as the Taylor errors predicted.
The errors themselves: 0.00289, -0.00303, -7.04\times10^{-5}, -5.14\times10^{-5} at h = 0.1: the leading terms \pm0.0296h, -0.00705h^2, -0.00514h^2.


Vectorised over h as in Convergence and cost. N’‘(3) is computed from the differentiated logistic equation, N’’ = r N’ (1 - 2N/K). The ratio of errors at h and h/2 is 2^p, the cheapest way to confirm the order when the exact answer is known; without it, use the difference-ratio check from the recap slide. The forward and backward ratios are not exactly 2 because the O(h^2) terms are still visible at h = 0.1.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Each stencil has its own V
text:
Each stencil has its own V

Rounding hits the second derivative hardest: it divides by h^2, not h. Its V is shifted far to the right.

Three curves, same OD function at t = 3. Right side: truncation, slopes 1, 2 and 2. Left side: rounding, slope -1 for the first-derivative formulas and -2 for the second derivative. The dotted lines mark eps^(1/2), eps^(1/3) and eps^(1/4), the rule-of-thumb best steps from the next slide; each is close to the bottom of its V. Note how much worse the second derivative is at small h: at h = 1e-8, where the forward difference is at its best, the second difference is wrong by about 1.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: The best step: balance the two errors
text:
The best step: balance the two errors
Truncation \approx C h^p, rounding \approx \varepsilon |N| / h^k for the k-th derivative. Setting them equal: h^* \approx \varepsilon^{1/(p+k)}, \qquad \text{best error} \approx \varepsilon^{p/(p+k)} \qquad (\text{if } C \text{ and } |N| \text{ are of order } 1).

Higher order and a larger step: the central difference wins twice.
Steps are relative: use h = \varepsilon^{1/3}\max(|t|, 1). Time in seconds (t = 10\,800 s) or a rate constant of size 10^{-4} needs a step scaled to it.


Derivation for the central case: minimise C h^2 + eps |N| / h; derivative 2 C h - eps |N| / h^2 = 0 gives h = (eps |N| / 2C)^(1/3). With C = |N’’’|/6 = 0.007 and |N| = 0.39 that is 1.8e-5, close to eps^(1/3) = 6e-6; the rule of thumb ignores the constants because they are rarely known. For the second derivative the rounding term is about 4 eps |N| / h^2 (weights 1, 2, 1). The relative step matters as soon as t (or a parameter) is far from 1: for a rate constant of 1e-4, an absolute step of 6e-6 changes it by 6 percent (truncation error), and for t = 10800 s, the truncation-optimal step is scaled up in proportion. Library codes scale every step by the size of the variable.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Failure: the second derivative with a tiny step
text:
Failure: the second derivative with a tiny step
h   <- 10^-(2:8)
sec <- (od(t0 + h) - 2 * od(t0) + od(t0 - h)) / h^2
print(data.frame(h, sec, err = abs(sec - d2)), digits = 3)
#       h     sec      err
# 1 1e-02  0.0592 5.14e-07
# 2 1e-03  0.0592 5.21e-09
# 3 1e-04  0.0592 7.82e-09
# 4 1e-05  0.0592 9.07e-07
# 5 1e-06  0.0591 1.49e-04
# 6 1e-07  0.0500 9.25e-03
# 7 1e-08 -0.5551 6.14e-01

At h = 10^{-8}, the step that is best for the forward difference, the curvature is -0.56: ten times too large, with the wrong sign. “Growth is slowing down”, confidently and falsely.
Check: vary h by factors of 10. The answer must stay put over a range of h; if it drifts or changes sign, you are in the rounding regime.


A typical way to hit this: copying the step 1e-8 (or sqrt(eps)) from a first-derivative code into a second-derivative code. The numerator is the difference of three numbers that agree in about 15 digits, so it is pure rounding noise of size 1e-16, divided by 1e-16. The check costs a few extra evaluations and is always worth it: a derivative estimate that is stable over two or three decades of h can be trusted; one that changes with h cannot. Same check as the difference ratios from Convergence and cost, without needing the exact answer.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Richardson extrapolation
The central difference has an error made of even powers only: D(h) = N' + c_2 h^2 + c_4 h^4 + \dots, \qquad D(h/2) = N' + \tfrac{c_2}{4} h^2 + \tfrac{c_4}{16} h^4 + \dots Take 4 D(h/2) - D(h): the h^2 term cancels. Divide by 3: R(h) = \frac{4 D(h/2) - D(h)}{3} = N' + O(h^4).
D <- function(h) (od(t0 + h) - od(t0 - h)) / (2 * h)
c(D(0.1), D(0.05), (4 * D(0.05) - D(0.1)) / 3) - exact      # errors
# [1] -7.043731e-05 -1.761183e-05 -3.336916e-09

Two second-order estimates with errors 10^{-4} and 10^{-5} give one with error 3\times10^{-9}. Fourth order, from the same four function values.
Repeat on the R’s (now dividing by 16 - 1, then 64 - 1): a table of ever higher order. Four levels from h = 0.4: error 3\times10^{-13}.


Richardson extrapolation is “use the known shape of the error to remove it”. We do not know c2, but we know how it scales with h, so two estimates are enough to eliminate it. This only works if the error really is c2 h^2 + …, i.e. in the truncation regime and for a smooth function. The repeated version is a triangular table, column j removing the h^(2j) term with weights 4j/(4j - 1) and -1/(4^j - 1); exercise C3 builds it. The same idea turns the trapezoid rule into Romberg integration in the next unit, Numerical integration.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
What numDeriv::grad does
library(numDeriv)
grad(od, 3) - exact                       # Richardson, the default
# [1] 2.060019e-13
grad(od, 3, method = "simple") - exact    # one forward difference
# [1] 2.960551e-06

grad takes central differences at a relative step h = 10^{-4}|x| and at h/2, h/4, h/8 (8 evaluations of f per variable) and runs the Richardson table: 12–13 correct digits.
method = "simple": one forward difference with h = 10^{-4}, error \approx 0.0296 \times 10^{-4}.
Python: scipy.differentiate.derivative (adaptive, Richardson-like); scipy.optimize.approx_fprime is a plain forward difference.
When Richardson fails: if f is not smooth (an if, abs, interpolated data, an adaptive ODE solver), or noisy, the error is not c_2h^2 + \dots and the extrapolation can make it worse.


numDeriv’s defaults: method.args = list(d = 1e-4, r = 4, v = 2): initial relative step d, r rounds of extrapolation, step reduction factor v. The large starting step keeps the whole table out of the rounding regime, and the extrapolation supplies the accuracy instead of a tiny step. That is the main practical lesson: accuracy should come from the formula’s order, not from shrinking h. On noise: the weights 4/3 and -1/3 add up to 1 but their absolute values sum to 5/3, so random errors in D grow at every level.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Measured data: the noise replaces \varepsilon
Each measurement is y_i = N(t_i) + e_i, noise sd \sigma = 0.005. The central difference of the noise has sd \frac{\sqrt{2}\,\sigma}{2\,\Delta t} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt2\,\Delta t} = \frac{0.005}{\sqrt2 \cdot \tfrac16} = 0.021 \text{ OD/h}.
set.seed(1)
t  <- seq(0, 10, by = 1/6)                            # every 10 min
y  <- round(od(t) + rnorm(length(t), sd = 0.005), 3)  # plate reader, 3 decimals
i  <- 2:(length(t) - 1)
cen <- (y[i + 1] - y[i - 1]) / (2 / 6)                # central, h = 10 min
sqrt(mean((cen - gr(t[i]))^2))                        # rms error
# [1] 0.02030602

The same \varepsilon/h term as before, with \varepsilon|N| \approx 10^{-16} replaced by \sigma = 5\times10^{-3}: 13 orders of magnitude larger.
Measuring more often makes it worse: every 2 min, the noise in N' is 0.11 OD/h, almost half the peak growth rate.


The derivation: the difference of two independent errors has variance 2 sigma^2; dividing by 2 dt divides the sd by 2 dt. The measured rms error 0.0203 matches the predicted 0.0212. Differentiation is an ill-conditioned operation in the language of Error, conditioning and stability: a small change in the data (0.005) gives a large change in the derivative, and the smaller the spacing, the larger the amplification. That is the opposite of most students’ intuition that more data is always better. More data helps only if we use it to average, which is what the next slides do. If you then compute the specific growth rate N’/N (or the slope of log OD), the noise is further divided by N, so it is worst at the low ODs of early growth.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
The V again, with noise
Use a wider central difference: \dfrac{y_{i+k} - y_{i-k}}{2k\,\Delta t}, half-width h = k\,\Delta t. Noise \sigma/(\sqrt2 h) falls, truncation \tfrac{h^2}{6}|N'''| grows.

Best near h = 40 min (k = 4): rms error 0.0053, four times smaller than neighbours. Predicted: h^* = \big(3\sigma / (\sqrt2\,|N'''|)\big)^{1/3} \approx 0.5 h.

Exactly the V of the recap slide, on a much larger scale: truncation on the right, noise on the left, and an optimal step that is now about half an hour instead of 1e-8. The formula for h* is the same balance as for rounding, with eps|N| replaced by sigma/sqrt(2) and |N’’‘| taken at its largest, 0.077 at the inflection point. In practice you do not know sigma or N’’’ precisely, but the lesson is robust: with noisy data the best stencil is much wider than the sampling interval. The price: fewer points at the ends (k values lost on each side) and some blurring of sharp features.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Smooth first, then differentiate
Fit a smooth curve to all the data, then differentiate the curve. A smoothing spline (Splines, Part 6) picks its smoothness from the data:
fit <- smooth.spline(t, y)                 # smoothness chosen by GCV
d   <- predict(fit, t, deriv = 1)$y        # derivative of the spline
sqrt(mean((d - gr(t))^2))                  # rms error
# [1] 0.004708606
c(max(d), t[which.max(d)])                 # max growth rate and when
# [1] 0.2366499 4.0000000

rms error 0.0047, and a value at every time point, ends included. Maximum growth rate 0.237 OD/h at 4.0 h (true: 0.240 at 3.92 h); raw central differences gave 0.270.
Python: scipy.interpolate.make_smoothing_spline, then .derivative().
Alternatives: a local polynomial fit (Savitzky–Golay), or fit a growth model and differentiate it (Part 9).


smooth.spline chooses its smoothing parameter by generalised cross-validation, which balances fit against roughness, the same bias-variance trade-off as the stencil width, made automatically. predict with deriv = 1 differentiates the fitted cubic pieces exactly. How smoothing splines work is the topic of Splines. Fitting a parametric model (logistic, Gompertz) and differentiating it is the most accurate option when the model is right, and the most misleading when it is wrong; that is Part 9 (Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting).

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Comparing the three


Raw neighbours (grey): noisy. Wider stencil (blue) and spline (orange): close to the truth, both slightly flatten the peak.
The spline is least reliable at the ends (here 0.056 instead of 0.038 at t = 0).
Check: compute the derivative with two different smoothing levels (stencil widths, spline df). Features that survive both are real; features that move are noise.


All smoothing trades noise for bias: a peak gets lower and wider. The spline errs at the ends because there are no data beyond them to pin down the slope; this is where the first growth rate (lag phase) is estimated, so be careful when reporting it. The two-smoothing-level check is the noisy-data version of “vary h by factors of 10”. Never report a derivative of raw data without having looked at this plot.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Gradients for fitting
Fit (r, K, N_0) to the plate-reader data by maximum likelihood (Gaussian noise, \sigma = 0.005): \ell(r, K, N_0) = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i \big(y_i - N(t_i; r, K, N_0)\big)^2. The gradient \nabla\ell = (\partial\ell/\partial r, \partial\ell/\partial K, \partial\ell/\partial N_0): one central difference per parameter, nudging only that one.
logistic <- function(t, r, K, N0) K / (1 + (K / N0 - 1) * exp(-r * t))
loglik <- function(th) -sum((y - logistic(t, th[1], th[2], th[3]))^2) / (2 * 0.005^2)
cen_grad <- function(f, x, h = 6e-6) sapply(seq_along(x), function(j) {
  e <- replace(numeric(length(x)), j, h)          # nudge parameter j only
  (f(x + e) - f(x - e)) / (2 * h) })
th <- c(r = 0.75, K = 1.15, N0 = 0.06)            # a point on the way to the optimum
cen_grad(loglik, th)
# [1]  42388.45  57583.61 109411.83

Relative error against the analytic gradient: forward (h = 10^{-8}) 10^{-7}–10^{-6}; central 10^{-11}–10^{-7}; numDeriv::grad 10^{-12}.
Cost: p + 1 (forward), 2p (central), 8p (numDeriv) evaluations of \ell for p parameters.


A partial derivative is an ordinary derivative with the other parameters held fixed, so every formula of this lecture applies one coordinate at a time. This is the same construction as the finite-difference Jacobian in Newton for systems of equations, applied to a scalar function. The gradient components are large (1e4 to 1e5) because sigma is small; what matters is the relative error. The analytic gradient is in the exercise (C6). For three parameters the cost does not matter; for an ODE model with 50 parameters where one evaluation takes a second, 100 or 400 seconds per gradient does.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Failure: optim’s default gradient
Without a gradient, optim uses central differences with a fixed absolute step ndeps = 1e-3.
fit1 <- optim(th, loglik, method = "BFGS", control = list(fnscale = -1))
fit2 <- optim(th, loglik, gr = function(p) grad(loglik, p),
              method = "BFGS", control = list(fnscale = -1))
rbind(default = fit1$par, numDeriv = fit2$par)
#                  r        K         N0
# default  0.7948541 1.202606 0.05085940
# numDeriv 0.7954268 1.202457 0.05076077
grad(loglik, fit1$par)                    # should be ~0 at the maximum
# [1] 48.205320  7.205445 -8.363963

h = 10^{-3} is 2 % of N_0 = 0.05: at the true maximum the default gradient is still 290 in the N_0 direction. BFGS stops at the wrong place.
Here the error is about \tfrac15 of a standard error. For a parameter of size 10^{-3} (a rate constant in /s) the step is the size of the parameter.
Check: evaluate an accurate gradient at the returned optimum. Fix: pass gr, or set parscale/ndeps to the parameter sizes.


fnscale = -1 makes optim maximise. The default-gradient run stops after 16 gradient evaluations at a point where the true gradient is (48, 7, -8), compared with 1e-4 for the run with the numDeriv gradient. The parameter differences (6e-4 in r, 1e-4 in N0) are about 0.17 standard errors (standard errors 0.0035 and 0.0006 from the Hessian), so the conclusions here do not change. But it is a silent wrong answer, and it gets worse the further parameters are from size 1. scipy.optimize.minimize uses a relative forward step instead, so it fails differently (fewer digits, not a biased gradient). Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters (Part 9) uses the Hessian, again by finite differences.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Optional: the complex step
If f is a formula that also works for complex numbers, step in the imaginary direction: f(x + ih) = f(x) + ih f'(x) - \tfrac{h^2}{2}f''(x) - \dots \;\Longrightarrow\; f'(x) = \frac{\operatorname{Im} f(x + ih)}{h} + O(h^2).
Im(od(t0 + 1e-20i)) / 1e-20 - exact       # 1e-20i: the complex number 10^-20 i
# [1] -2.775558e-17

No subtraction, so no cancellation: h = 10^{-20} is fine, and the result is exact to rounding.
Only for code that accepts complex input: no abs, max, if (x > 0), compiled solvers. One derivative per evaluation.


Optional slide; complex numbers are not assumed knowledge. The idea: the real part carries f(x), the imaginary part carries h f’(x), and they never have to be subtracted from each other. The O(h^2) truncation term is h^2 f’’’ / 6 times 1e-40: invisible. In R, exp, log, sin and arithmetic all work on complex numbers, so the logistic formula works unchanged. It breaks as soon as the code compares numbers or calls something that is real-only. It is a stepping stone to the next slide: carrying a derivative along with the value through the computation.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Automatic differentiation: what Stan, JAX and torch do
text:
Automatic differentiation: what Stan, JAX and torch do
A program is a chain of elementary steps (+, \times, exp, …), each with a known derivative. Automatic differentiation (AD) applies the chain rule to the numbers as the program runs.









finite differences
AD




accuracy
half to two-thirds of the digits
exact up to rounding: no h


gradient of p parameters
p+1 to 8p evaluations
reverse mode: about 2–4 evaluations, any p


needs
only f as a black box
code written in an AD-aware library




Forward mode: carry (value, derivative) through every step; one pass per parameter.
Reverse mode (backpropagation): record the steps, then run the chain rule backwards once for the whole gradient.
Stan (gradients for HMC sampling), TMB/RTMB, JAX, PyTorch, Julia. A log-likelihood with 10 000 parameters: AD is the only option.


One slide, no code: the point is to know what these tools do and why they exist. Forward mode on the logistic: v1 = -r t, v2 = exp(v1), v3 = 1 + A v2, v4 = K / v3; carrying derivatives with respect to t gives dv1 = -r, dv2 = v2 dv1, dv3 = A dv2, dv4 = -K dv3 / v3^2 (exercise B7 does this by hand). Reverse mode is why deep learning is possible: a network with a million weights gets its whole gradient for the price of a few forward passes. Its cost is memory: every intermediate value is stored for the backward pass. For an ODE model inside a likelihood, the AD-aware tools differentiate through the solver (sensitivity equations or adjoints). Finite differences remain the right tool for black-box code and for checking an AD or hand-written gradient.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Checklist: detecting derivative trouble

Value changes when h changes by 10× → rounding regime (too small) or truncation (too large). Find the plateau.
Step not scaled to the variable → use h = \varepsilon^{1/3}\max(|x|, 1) (central), or parscale in optim.
Second derivative with a first-derivative step → use h \approx \varepsilon^{1/4}, never 10^{-8}.
Derivative of measured data → never difference neighbours; widen the stencil or smooth, and compare two smoothing levels.
Negative growth rates mid-growth, spiky curves → noise, not biology.
Optimiser stops with a non-zero gradient → check with numDeriv::grad at the result; supply an analytic or AD gradient.
Hand-written gradient → compare with a finite-difference gradient; agreement to ~10^{-7} relative, not \sim 1.
Function with if, abs, interpolation, or an adaptive ODE solve → not smooth: no Richardson, larger h.


Every item corresponds to a failure shown in this lecture or the exercise. The gradient check (last-but-one item) is standard practice before trusting any hand-coded or AD gradient: a sign error or missing factor gives a relative difference of order 1, not 1e-7. The last item: an adaptive ODE solver’s output changes in small jumps when a parameter changes, because the step sequence changes; its tolerance (say 1e-6) plays the role of eps, so the best step is around sqrt(1e-6) = 1e-3, not 1e-8.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Summary

Stencils from Taylor: forward/backward O(h), central O(h^2), second derivative \tfrac{N(t+h) - 2N(t) + N(t-h)}{h^2}, O(h^2). Any stencil: match Taylor terms with a small linear system.
Best step balances truncation Ch^p against rounding \varepsilon/h^k: \varepsilon^{1/2} (forward), \varepsilon^{1/3} (central), \varepsilon^{1/4} (second derivative). Steps are relative to the variable.
Richardson: \tfrac{4D(h/2) - D(h)}{3} removes the h^2 error; repeated, it gives 12–13 digits (numDeriv::grad). Needs a smooth function.
Measured data: noise \sigma replaces \varepsilon, and \sigma/h is huge. Widen the stencil or smooth first (Splines); check with two smoothing levels.
Gradients for fitting: one difference per parameter; watch the step size relative to each parameter (optim’s ndeps). AD gives exact gradients at the cost of a few evaluations.

Next: Numerical integration, the opposite operation: integrating averages the noise away, and Richardson returns as Romberg.

The single idea of the unit: every derivative estimate divides a difference by a small number, and that amplifies whatever error is in the values, rounding or measurement noise. The stencils tell us how fast truncation falls; the balance tells us where to stop. The second-derivative stencil returns in Part 10 as the diffusion term. Numerical integration is the friendly counterpart: errors average out instead of being amplified.

title: Exercise: the SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Explore
The demo below solves the deconvolution of the lecture in your browser: the same signature \(S\) (CD4T and CD8T differ by 2 % on genes 1 and 2), true proportions \(p = (0.30, 0.15, 0.15, 0.10, 0.30)\), and a bulk sample \(b = b_0\,(1 + s \cdot \text{noise})\). With lecture pattern the noise is the fixed \(\sin(37g)\) of the slides, so at \(s = 5\%\) you get the slide numbers; random draws \(N(0,1)\) noise instead, and new random sample draws another one. The SVD is computed by one-sided Jacobi (rotations of pairs of columns of \(S\), never \(S^TS\)).

Panel (a): the estimate for this sample (bars), the truth (dashed) and the estimates from 100 further samples with fresh random noise of the same size (dots; arrows count dots off the scale). The last group is CD4 + CD8.
Panel (b): the filter factors \(f_i\) of the chosen method against \(\sigma\), with the five singular values as circles.
Panel (c): the error to expect over the noise, split into bias \(\|E[x] - p\|\) (what the method gets wrong without noise) and noise \(\sqrt{E\|x - E[x]\|^2}\) (the spread of the dots), against \(\lambda\) or \(k\); total \(= \sqrt{\text{bias}^2 + \text{noise}^2}\). Both use the truth, which only a simulation knows.




E1. (noise is divided by \(\sigma_i\)) Start with least squares at 5 % noise. Read the estimate, the expected noise and how many dots fall off the scale for CD4T and CD8T. Then set the noise to 1 % and to 0. How does the expected noise depend on \(s\)? Which estimates do the dots leave alone, and what does the readout give as the multiplier \(f_5/\sigma_5\) of \(u_5^Tb\)?






Answer E1





At 5 %: \(x = (0.543, -0.092, 0.149, 0.099, 0.299)\), as on the slides; expected noise 1.202, and 32 of 100 dots fall off the scale (\(-0.6\) to \(1.2\)) for CD4T and for CD8T. At 1 % the noise is 0.240 and the estimate \((0.349, 0.102, \dots)\); at 0 the estimate is exactly \(p\). The noise is proportional to \(s\) (1.202 / 5 = 0.240): least squares has no bias, only noise. The dots for B, NK, Mono and CD4 + CD8 stay in a tight band (CD4 + CD8 = 0.451 at 5 %): the noise lands only along \(v_5 \approx (1, -1, 0, 0, 0)/\sqrt2\), which changes the split but not the total. The multiplier is \(1/\sigma_5 = 1/2.87 = 0.348\), against at most \(1/269 = 0.0037\) for the other components: component 5 amplifies noise about 90 times more.



E2. (truncation: bias against noise) Back at 5 % noise, choose truncated SVD and move \(k\) from 5 down to 1. Note \(\|x - p\|\), \(\|Sx - b\|\), and the expected bias and noise for each \(k\). Where does the step in panel (b) sit for \(k = 4\)? Which \(k\) gives the smallest expected error, and which \(k\) would the residual alone point to?






Answer E2

These are the lecture’s table. For \(k = 4\) the step lies between \(\sigma_5 = 2.87\) and \(\sigma_4 = 269\), so only \(\sigma_5\) gets \(f = 0\). Dropping component 5 cuts the noise from 1.202 to 0.011 at the price of a bias of 0.106: that bias is the equal split \(0.226/0.226\) instead of \(0.30/0.15\), the part of \(p\) along \(v_5\) that TSVD sets to 0. Fewer components only add bias. The smallest expected error is at \(k = 4\) (0.107), and the residual says the same without the truth: it drops steeply until \(k = 4\) and then barely moves (9.71 to 9.62). All dots for CD4T and CD8T now sit on top of each other: very stable, and wrong in the same way every time.



E3. (ridge: a smooth filter) Choose ridge and move \(\lambda\) from 0.1 to 1000. Read \(f_5\) and the expected bias and noise at \(\lambda = 1\), 10, 31.6 and 316. Where do the bias and noise curves cross, and where is the total smallest? At \(\lambda = 10\), compare the error of the lecture sample with the expected error, then click random and new random sample a few times. What happens to all five proportions at \(\lambda = 316\) and 1000?






Answer E3





\(\lambda = 1\): \(f_5 = 0.892\), bias 0.011, noise 1.072. \(\lambda = 10\): \(f_5 = 0.076\), bias 0.098, noise 0.092, total 0.135: the curves cross close to \(\lambda = 10\). \(\lambda = 31.6\): \(f_5 = 0.008\), bias 0.105, noise 0.015, total 0.106, the smallest (the readout’s “smallest total”), as good as TSVD with \(k = 4\). \(\lambda = 316\): total 0.187, now all bias. The lecture sample at \(\lambda = 10\) has \(\|x - p\| = 0.072\), better than the expected 0.135: its noise pattern happens to push the split towards the truth (the lecture called this luck). Random samples (seeds 1–3) give 0.091, 0.092 and 0.067: the dots show a spread of about \(\pm0.07\) around 0.23 (CD4) and 0.22 (CD8), close to the equal split. At \(\lambda = 316\) (\(f_1 \ldots f_4\) are no longer near 1) every proportion shrinks, CD4 + CD8 = 0.384 and Mono 0.165; at 1000 the estimate is \((0.073, 0.073, 0.026, 0.022, 0.038)\) and the residual 193. Too much ridge is bias in everything, not just the split.



E4. (how much regularisation depends on the noise) Keep ridge and read the readout’s “smallest total” at noise 0.5 %, 1 %, 5 %, 10 % and 20 %. How does the best \(\lambda\) move, and why?






Answer E4





The best \(\lambda\) is about 3.2 at 0.5 %, 6.3 at 1 %, 32 at 5 %, 50 at 10 % and 63 at 20 % (total errors 0.080, 0.097, 0.106, 0.108, 0.115). More noise means component 5 must be damped harder, so the step \(\sigma = \lambda\) in panel (b) moves right, away from \(\sigma_5 = 2.87\). It can never pass \(\sigma_4 = 269\) without destroying the well-determined proportions, so even at 20 % noise the best \(\lambda\) stays far below it. With less noise, a smaller \(\lambda\) lets part of the true split through (\(f_5 = 0.45\) at \(\lambda = 3.2\)), and the best error drops below the 0.106 of TSVD. Regularisation must be matched to the noise level, which is why \(\lambda\) is chosen from the data (residual, L-curve) rather than fixed once.



E5. (better data, not better maths) Press reset. Move CD8 differs by (the difference between CD8T and CD4T on genes 1 and 2) to 0 (identical columns), then to 10 % and 30 %. Read \(\sigma_5\), \(\kappa\), the least-squares estimate and its expected noise. At 30 %, which method has the smallest expected error now?






Answer E5





At 0: \(\sigma_5 = 0\) and \(\kappa = \infty\). The demo, like pinv, drops singular values below the rounding tolerance, so “least squares” returns the minimum-norm answer \((0.226, 0.226, 0.149, 0.099, 0.299)\), identical to TSVD \(k = 4\). At 10 %: \(\sigma_5 = 14.4\), \(\kappa = 44.8\), \(x = (0.355, 0.097, \dots)\), expected noise 0.241. At 30 %: \(\sigma_5 = 43.0\), \(\kappa = 15.0\), \(x = (0.323, 0.128, \dots)\), noise 0.081, so least squares now beats TSVD \(k = 4\) (0.108), which still throws away the split. Ridge with \(\lambda \approx 32\) is best (0.065), and at \(\lambda = 10\) the estimate \((0.318, 0.133)\) is within 0.02 of the truth. \(\sigma_5\) grows in proportion to the difference (2.87 per 2 %), and the noise along \(v_5\) falls as \(1/\sigma_5\). A signature with genes that really separate the two cell types does what no choice of \(k\) or \(\lambda\) can.

title: Exercise: structure — symmetric, banded, sparse
text:
Explore
The demo below runs Cholesky on the pattern of a sparse symmetric matrix, one column at a time, and only tracks which entries of \(L\) become non-zero (it assumes no lucky cancellation). Panel (a) shows the pattern with rows and columns in elimination order: blue entries are non-zeros of \(A\), vermillion entries are fill-in, and entries outlined in black were created by the last step. The finished rows and columns are faded; the box marks the next pivot. Panel (b) shows the same matrix as a network: one node per unknown (gene or cell), one link per non-zero pair. The number in a node is its place in the elimination order. Eliminating a node links all its remaining neighbours to each other, and every new link is a fill-in entry.
The counters give the non-zeros of \(A\), of \(L\) so far, the fill-in so far, and the operations so far: a column with \(c\) non-zeros below the pivot costs \((c + 1)^2\) (one square root, \(c\) divisions, and \(c(c+1)/2\) multiply-subtract pairs), which gives about \(n^3/3\) for a full matrix. The table compares the five orderings for the current matrix, and for the same kind of matrix with \(n = 1000\) (the 2D grid: \(30 \times 30\)). Min degree always eliminates the node with fewest remaining neighbours next; RCM (reverse Cuthill–McKee) numbers the nodes in breadth-first sweeps, which keeps the non-zeros near the diagonal.



E1. (the hub first) The arrow matrix with \(n = 8\) genes is selected, hub first (natural order). Click step ▶ once. How many neighbours does the pivot have, how many fill-in entries appear, and what does \(L\) look like at the end (click all)? Now choose reversed (hub last) and step through all 8 columns. Compare nnz(\(L\)) and the operations, and the column for \(n = 1000\) with C7.






Answer E1





Hub first: the pivot (the hub) has \(c = 7\) neighbours, all \(7 \cdot 6/2 = 21\) pairs of leaves get linked, and all 21 are new. That single step fills the whole lower right \(7 \times 7\) block; in panel (b) every leaf is now linked to every other. At the end \(L\) has 36 non-zeros, the full lower triangle \(8 \cdot 9/2\), with 21 fill-in, and costs \(1^2 + 2^2 + \dots + 8^2 = 204\) operations. Hub last: each leaf has only the hub as neighbour (\(c = 1\), nothing to link), so no step creates fill-in; \(L\) has \(15 = 2n - 1\) non-zeros (the non-zeros of the lower triangle of \(A\)) and costs 29 operations. For \(n = 1000\) the table gives 500 500 against 1999, the numbers of C7.



E2. (let the ordering choose) Stay with the arrow matrix and try shuffled, min degree and RCM. Where does the hub land in each ordering (look at its number in panel (b)), and how much fill-in does each give? Then set \(n = 30\) and compare natural with min degree.






Answer E2





Shuffled puts the hub 4th: the three leaves before it cost nothing, then the hub still has \(c = 4\) neighbours and links them, \(4 \cdot 3/2 = 6\) fill-ins (nnz(\(L\)) 21 instead of 15). The fill-in only depends on how many neighbours the hub has left when it goes. Min degree eliminates the leaves first (degree 1) and keeps the hub to the end (7th, with only the last leaf left), and RCM numbers the hub 7th too: both give 15 non-zeros, no fill-in, like hub last. At \(n = 30\): natural has 465 non-zeros and 406 fill-ins and costs 9455 operations; min degree 59 non-zeros, no fill-in, 117 operations. This is what Cholesky(A, perm = TRUE) does for you: it finds a fill-reducing ordering before it factorises.



E3. (a row of cells) Choose tridiagonal, \(n = 12\) (the morphogen in a row of cells), natural order, and click play. Does any step create fill-in? Then choose shuffled and step through. What happens in panel (b) when a cell in the middle of the row is eliminated, and how many fill-ins does that give at most? Repeat with band (width 2).






Answer E3





Natural order: each pivot has one remaining neighbour (the next cell), so there is nothing to link; no fill-in, \(L\) has \(2n - 1 = 23\) non-zeros, 45 operations, \(4(n - 1) + 1\): the Thomas algorithm, \(O(n)\). Shuffled: eliminating a cell whose two neighbours are both still there links those two neighbours, one new link that jumps over the eliminated cell. That is at most one fill-in per step, so the fill stays small (5 here, nnz(\(L\)) 28, 70 operations; 2986 instead of 1999 at \(n = 1000\)), but the pattern in panel (a) is scattered, not a band, so Thomas could not be used. The band of width 2 behaves the same: no fill-in in natural order (33 non-zeros, 95 operations), 7 fill-ins shuffled. Elimination never fills outside the band when you go along the row.



E4. (a sheet of cells) Choose 2D grid with side 6 (36 cells, numbered row by row) in natural order. Click step ▶ six times, eliminating the first row of cells. Where does the fill-in go in panel (a)? Click all and read nnz(\(L\)). Then compare min degree and RCM, also for the \(30 \times 30\) grid. Can any ordering avoid fill-in here?






Answer E4





After the first row (6 steps) there are already 25 fill-ins. The first cell links its right neighbour to the cell below it; each later cell of the row links its right neighbour, the cell below it and the cells of the second row that earlier steps had already linked to it. In panel (a) all of this lands inside the band between the diagonal and the neighbour one row down (6 positions away), and the band fills up from the left. In natural order the whole band of width 6 fills in: \(L\) has 221 non-zeros against 96 in the lower triangle of \(A\) (125 fill-in), and costs 1451 operations. Min degree: 167 non-zeros (71 fill-in), 845 operations; RCM: 191 and 1101. For \(30 \times 30\): 27 029 in natural order, the number on the lecture slide; min degree gives 10 351 (the lecture’s AMD gets 10 231), RCM 19 315. No ordering reaches zero: in a sheet, every cell has four neighbours, and eliminating one always links some of them that were not linked before. In 2D (and much more in 3D) some fill-in is unavoidable; that is where iterative solvers come in.

title: Exercise: power iteration and friends
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 2 × 2 matrix by hand, and read a Leslie matrix (long-term growth rate, stable age distribution) and a Markov chain (stationary distribution) in terms of them,
write power iteration with normalisation and a residual-based stopping rule, and check it against eigen(),
predict the number of iterations from \(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|\), measure the rate from an error plot, and recognise the two failures: \(|\lambda_2| = |\lambda_1|\) (no convergence) and \(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1| \approx 1\) (false convergence),
compute the Rayleigh quotient and explain why it doubles the digits for symmetric matrices,
use inverse iteration with a shift (factor once, solve many times) to find the eigenvalue nearest a chosen number.

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a pocket calculator. The code part checks the hand answers and then works with the fish population and the cell-state chain from the lecture.

title: Exercise: power iteration and friends
text:
Background
An eigenvector \(\mathbf v \ne \mathbf 0\) of a square matrix \(A\) satisfies \(A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v\); the number \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue. We order eigenvalues by size: \(|\lambda_1| \ge |\lambda_2| \ge \dots\)
Facts used below:

2 × 2 by hand. The eigenvalues solve \(\det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - (\text{trace})\lambda + \det A = 0\). For each \(\lambda\), solve \((A - \lambda I)\mathbf v = \mathbf 0\) (one equation is enough, the other is a multiple of it).
Leslie matrix. Fertilities \(F_i\) in the first row, survival probabilities \(s_i\) on the subdiagonal; \(\mathbf n_{t+1} = L\mathbf n_t\). The dominant eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) is the long-term growth rate per time step, and its eigenvector, rescaled to sum 1, is the stable age distribution.
Markov chain. \(P_{ij}\) = probability of moving from state \(i\) to state \(j\) in one step; rows sum to 1; proportions evolve as \(\mathbf p_{t+1} = \mathbf p_tP\) (row vector). The stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol\pi\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi\): it is the eigenvector of \(P^T\) for \(\lambda_1 = 1\), rescaled to sum 1.
Power iteration. \(\mathbf y = A\mathbf x_k\), estimate \(\lambda\), \(\mathbf x_{k+1} = \mathbf y/\|\mathbf y\|\). For nonnegative matrices normalise by the sum (\(\mathbf x\) = proportions, estimate \(\lambda \approx \mathrm{sum}(A\mathbf x_k)\)); in general by the 2-norm.
Rate. If \(\mathbf x_0 = c_1\mathbf v_1 + c_2\mathbf v_2 + \dots\) with \(c_1 \ne 0\), then \(A^k\mathbf x_0 = \lambda_1^k\big(c_1\mathbf v_1 + c_2(\lambda_2/\lambda_1)^k\mathbf v_2 + \dots\big)\): the error falls by about \(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|\) per step (linear convergence), so one digit takes \(1/\log_{10}(|\lambda_1/\lambda_2|)\) steps. No convergence if \(|\lambda_2| = |\lambda_1|\).
Stopping. Stop when the residual \(\|A\mathbf x - \lambda\mathbf x\|\) is small. If successive changes shrink by a factor \(c\) per step, the remaining error is about \(\text{change}\cdot c/(1-c)\), which is much larger than the change when \(c\) is near 1.
Rayleigh quotient. \(R(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^TA\mathbf x / \mathbf x^T\mathbf x\), equal to \(\lambda\) for an eigenvector. For symmetric \(A\), an error \(\delta\) in \(\mathbf x\) gives an error of order \(\delta^2\) in \(R(\mathbf x)\).
Inverse iteration. \((A - \sigma I)^{-1}\) has the same eigenvectors as \(A\) and eigenvalues \(1/(\lambda_i - \sigma)\). Power iteration with it (one linear solve per step) finds the eigenvalue nearest the shift \(\sigma\), at rate \(|\lambda_\text{nearest} - \sigma| / |\lambda_\text{next nearest} - \sigma|\). Factor \(A - \sigma I\) once; then each step costs only a forward and back substitution.

The basic tools in each language:

RPythonRust


L <- matrix(0, 4, 4)
L[1, ] <- c(0, 1.5, 4, 5)                  # offspring per fish of each age
L[cbind(2:4, 1:3)] <- c(0.3, 0.6, 0.5)     # survival to the next age
ev <- eigen(L)
ev$values
# [1]  1.1773586+0.000000i -0.2662888+0.722404i -0.2662888-0.722404i
# [4] -0.6447810+0.000000i
Mod(ev$values)
# [1] 1.1773586 0.7699203 0.7699203 0.6447810
v <- Re(ev$vectors[, 1])
v / sum(v)                                 # stable age distribution
# [1] 0.69453711 0.17697339 0.09018836 0.03830114


import numpy as np

L = np.zeros((4, 4))
L[0, :] = [0, 1.5, 4, 5]                   # offspring per fish of each age
L[[1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 2]] = [0.3, 0.6, 0.5]  # survival to the next age
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(L)
order = np.argsort(-np.abs(vals))          # eig does not sort: largest |lambda| first
vals, vecs = vals[order], vecs[:, order]
print(vals)
# [ 1.17735856+0.j         -0.2662888 +0.72240402j -0.2662888 -0.72240402j
#  -0.64478097+0.j        ]
print(np.abs(vals))
# [1.17735856 0.76992031 0.76992031 0.64478097]
v = vecs[:, 0].real
print(v / v.sum())                         # stable age distribution
# [0.69453711 0.17697339 0.09018836 0.03830114]


// rust/examples/power_iteration_background.rs  —  cargo run --example power_iteration_background
// Background: eigenvalues of the fish Leslie matrix with nalgebra.
// nalgebra has no general (nonsymmetric) eigenvector routine, so we only get
// the eigenvalues here; the eigenvector comes from power iteration (C1).
use nalgebra::DMatrix;

fn main() {
    let l = DMatrix::from_row_slice(4, 4, &[
        0.0, 1.5, 4.0, 5.0,      // offspring per fish of each age
        0.3, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0,      // survival to the next age
        0.0, 0.6, 0.0, 0.0,
        0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.0,
    ]);
    let mut ev: Vec<_> = l.complex_eigenvalues().iter().cloned().collect();
    ev.sort_by(|a, b| b.norm().partial_cmp(&a.norm()).unwrap()); // largest |lambda| first
    for z in &ev {
        println!("{:.7} {:+.7}i   |lambda| = {:.7}", z.re, z.im, z.norm());
    }
}

// Output:
// 1.1773586 +0.0000000i   |lambda| = 1.1773586
// -0.2662888 +0.7224040i   |lambda| = 0.7699203
// -0.2662888 -0.7224040i   |lambda| = 0.7699203
// -0.6447810 +0.0000000i   |lambda| = 0.6447810



R’s eigen sorts by decreasing \(|\lambda|\); numpy’s np.linalg.eig does not sort, so sort yourself. Both return complex numbers for a nonsymmetric matrix and eigenvectors of length 1 with an arbitrary sign: rescale before you interpret them. nalgebra’s complex_eigenvalues gives eigenvalues only; for eigenvectors of a nonsymmetric matrix the Rust code below uses power and inverse iteration, written by hand. Rust prints numbers in its own format; the values agree with R and Python to the digits shown unless the text says otherwise.

title: Exercise: power iteration and friends
text:
By hand
B1. A two-age-class plant. A perennial plant has first-year plants (class 1) and older plants (class 2). First-year plants produce 0.6 seedlings each, older plants 0.9; 80 % of first-year plants survive to the next year, older plants all die: \[L = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.9 \\ 0.8 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\] (a) Find the characteristic polynomial and both eigenvalues. (b) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue, and check \(L\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v\). (c) What are the long-term growth rate and the stable stage distribution (as proportions)? (d) What is \(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|\)? About how many power iterations does one decimal digit take?
B2. Power iteration by hand. Same plant, start with older plants only: \(\mathbf x_0 = (0, 1)\). (a) Compute \(\mathbf x_1, \dots, \mathbf x_4\) without normalising (\(\mathbf x_{k} = L\mathbf x_{k-1}\)). For each \(k\), compute the growth of the total, \(\text{sum}(\mathbf x_k)/\text{sum}(\mathbf x_{k-1})\), and its error compared with \(\lambda_1\). (b) Compute the ratio of successive errors. What number does it approach, and why does the sign alternate? (c) Write \(\mathbf x_0\) as a combination of the eigenvectors from B1 and use it to predict the proportion of first-year plants after 10 years. How far is it from the stable distribution?
B3. A biennial plant. A biennial plant forms a rosette in its first year and flowers in its second year (4 seedlings per plant), then dies; 25 % of rosettes survive to flower: \(L = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ 0.25 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\). (a) Find the eigenvalues. What is \(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|\)? (b) Compute \(L^2\). Starting from 100 rosettes, \(\mathbf x_0 = (100, 0)\), what are \(\mathbf x_1, \mathbf x_2, \mathbf x_3\)? What does the power-iteration estimate \(\text{sum}(\mathbf x_k)/\text{sum}(\mathbf x_{k-1})\) do? (c) What is the growth per two years? Is there a stable stage distribution? (d) In a variant, 10 % of first-year plants flower early (fertility 0.4 in class 1): \(L = \begin{pmatrix} 0.4 & 4 \\ 0.25 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\). Find the eigenvalues and \(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|\). Does power iteration converge now?
B4. A two-state cell chain. Cells switch between proliferating (P) and quiescent (Q). Per day, a proliferating cell becomes quiescent with probability 0.1, a quiescent cell becomes proliferating with probability 0.2: \[P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}.\] (a) Find the stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol\pi\) from \(\boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi\) and \(\pi_1 + \pi_2 = 1\). (b) The eigenvalues of \(P\) (and of \(P^T\)) are 1 and \(\text{trace}(P) - 1\). Why? What is \(\lambda_2\)? (c) Start with proliferating cells only, \(\mathbf p_0 = (1, 0)\). Compute \(\mathbf p_1, \mathbf p_2, \mathbf p_3\) and the error in the first entry. By what factor does it shrink each day? (d) How many days until the error is below 0.01? (e) Another cell type switches with probabilities 0.001 and 0.002. What is \(\lambda_2\)? In a simulation the proportions change by only \(10^{-6}\) from one day to the next. Roughly how far from equilibrium are they?
B5. Rayleigh quotient. \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) (a covariance matrix of two traits) has eigenvalues 6 and 1 with eigenvectors \((2, 1)\) and \((1, -2)\). (a) For \(\mathbf x = (1, 0.45)\), compute \(A\mathbf x\), the sum ratio \(\text{sum}(A\mathbf x)/\text{sum}(\mathbf x)\) and the Rayleigh quotient \(\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x/\mathbf x^T\mathbf x\). Give the error of each. (b) Repeat for \(\mathbf x = (1, 0.495)\), which is 10 times closer to the eigenvector direction \((1, 0.5)\). By what factor did each error shrink? (c) Explain the difference in one sentence.
B6. Inverse iteration. Use the plant matrix of B1 (\(\lambda = 1.2, -0.6\)). (a) For the shifts \(\sigma = 1\), \(\sigma = 0\) and \(\sigma = -0.5\), give the eigenvalues of \((L - \sigma I)^{-1}\), the eigenvalue of \(L\) that inverse iteration finds, and the convergence rate. Compare with plain power iteration. (b) Do one step of inverse iteration with \(\sigma = 1\) from \(\mathbf x_0 = (0, 1)\): solve \((L - I)\mathbf y = \mathbf x_0\) by hand and rescale \(\mathbf y\) to proportions. Compare the error with one step of power iteration (B2). (c) What happens with the shift \(\sigma = 1.2\) exactly? Would the result still be useful in exact arithmetic? In floating point?

title: Exercise: power iteration and friends
text:
In code
C1. Power iteration. Write power_it(A, x, tol, maxit) that normalises by the sum, estimates \(\lambda\) as the growth of the total, stops when the residual \(\|A\mathbf x - \lambda\mathbf x\|\) falls below tol, and returns \(\lambda\), \(\mathbf x\), the number of iterations and the residual. (a) Apply it to the fish Leslie matrix (Background) starting from the stocked lake, \((0, 1000, 0, 0)\), with tol = 1e-10. Report the growth rate, the stable age distribution and the iteration count. (b) Compare with eigen() (Python: np.linalg.eig): how large are the differences in \(\lambda_1\) and in the distribution? (c) Check your answers to B1 with the plant matrix.
C2. The convergence rate. For the fish, run 60 power iterations from \((0, 1, 0, 0)\) and record the error in the estimate of \(\lambda_1\) and the largest error in the age distribution (take eigen() as the truth). (a) Plot both errors against \(k\) on a log scale (R: plot(..., log = "y"); Python: plt.semilogy). (b) Fit a straight line to \(\log_{10}\)(distribution error) for \(k = 10, \dots, 50\) and compare its slope with \(\log_{10}|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|\). (c) Predict how many iterations it takes to shrink an error of 1 to \(10^{-10}\). Compare with C1.
C3. Failures. (a) Make the semelparous fish of the lecture (first row \((0, 0, 0, 12)\)). Print \(|\lambda_i|\), run power_it with maxit = 200, and report the iteration count and the final residual. (b) Run power_it on the biennial plant of B3 and on its early-flowering variant. Compare with your hand answers. (c) Run 5000 steps of \(\mathbf x \leftarrow L\mathbf x\) for the fish without normalising. What do you get, and after roughly how many steps does it go wrong?
C4. The stationary distribution of cell states. Use the cell-state chain of the lecture, \(P\) = (0.80, 0.15, 0.05; 0.05, 0.90, 0.05; 0.05, 0.10, 0.85) (rows S, B, L). (a) Find \(\boldsymbol\pi\) three ways: 100 steps of \(\mathbf p \leftarrow \mathbf pP\) from \((1, 0, 0)\); the eigenvector of \(P^T\) from eigen(); and as a linear system: \((P^T - I)\boldsymbol\pi^T = \mathbf 0\) with the last equation replaced by \(\pi_1 + \pi_2 + \pi_3 = 1\). (b) The slow chain \(P_\text{slow} = I + 0.01(P - I)\): iterate from \((1, 0, 0)\) until the largest change in one step is below \(10^{-8}\). Report the number of steps and the true error. (c) Estimate the rate \(c\) from the last two changes and the remaining error from \(\text{change}\cdot c/(1-c)\) (fact 6). Compare with the true error.
C5. Rayleigh quotient against sum ratio. Run power iteration with 2-norm normalisation for 80 steps. At each step compute the sum ratio \(\text{sum}(A\mathbf x)/\text{sum}(\mathbf x)\) and the Rayleigh quotient \(\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x/\mathbf x^T\mathbf x\), and record the first iteration at which each is within \(10^{-10}\) of \(\lambda_1\). Do this for (a) the trait correlation matrix \(C\) = (1, 0.4, 0.3; 0.4, 1, 0.2; 0.3, 0.2, 1) (symmetric), starting from \((1, 0, 0)\), and (b) the fish Leslie matrix, starting from \((0, 1, 0, 0)\). Explain the difference with fact 7.
C6. Inverse iteration with a shift. Write inv_it(A, sigma, x, tol, maxit) that factors \(A - \sigma I\) once (R: Matrix::lu and solve; Python: scipy.linalg.lu_factor and lu_solve), normalises in the 2-norm, estimates \(\lambda\) with the Rayleigh quotient of \(A\), and stops on the residual. (a) Find the stationary distribution of the slow chain with \(\sigma = 1 + 10^{-6}\). How many iterations? Compare with C4(b). (b) Find \(\lambda_2\) of \(P^T\) and its eigenvector with \(\sigma = 0.82\), then try \(\sigma = 0.77\). Which eigenvalues do you get, in how many iterations? Explain with fact 8. (c) The deviation from equilibrium shrinks by \(\lambda_2\) per day. How many days after sorting does it take to fall to 1 % of its initial size?
C7. Rayleigh quotient iteration. Write rqi(A, x, tol, maxit): at each step set the shift to the current Rayleigh quotient, print it with 16 digits together with the residual, stop when the residual is below \(10^{-9}\), otherwise solve \((A - \sigma I)\mathbf y = \mathbf x\) and normalise. (a) Run it on \(C\) from \((1, 1, 1)\). How does the residual fall from step to step? (b) Run it from \((1, 0, 0)\) and from \((1, -1, 0)\). Which eigenvalues do you get? (c) What happens if you lower the tolerance to \(10^{-12}\) in (a)? Why?

title: Exercise: power iteration and friends
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 2 × 2 (B1, B3, B4, B5)





\(\det\begin{pmatrix} a-\lambda & b \\ c & d-\lambda\end{pmatrix} = (a-\lambda)(d-\lambda) - bc\). For an eigenvector, take the first row of \((A - \lambda I)\mathbf v = \mathbf 0\), \((a - \lambda)v_1 + bv_2 = 0\), and pick \(v_1\) to make the numbers nice. To check, multiply \(A\mathbf v\) and compare entry by entry with \(\lambda\mathbf v\). For a Markov chain, \(\boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi\) gives one useful equation, e.g. \(0.1\pi_1 = 0.2\pi_2\) (“flow out of P = flow into P”).









Hint 2 — the convergence rate (B2, B4, C2)





Error after \(k\) steps \(\approx C\,|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|^k\). To reach a factor \(10^{-d}\) you need \(k = d/\log_{10}|\lambda_1/\lambda_2|\) steps. For a straight-line fit of \(\log_{10}\) error against \(k\): R lm(log10(err) ~ k), Python np.polyfit(k, np.log10(err), 1); the slope is the first coefficient in Python and the second in R.









Hint 3 — matrix products and the Markov chain (C1, C4)





R: A %*% x is the matrix product; drop() turns a one-column matrix into a vector; for the row vector of proportions, p %*% P. eigen(t(P)) gives the eigenvectors of \(P^T\) as columns. Python: A @ x, p @ P, np.linalg.eig(P.T). For the linear system, solve(M, b) / np.linalg.solve.









Hint 4 — inverse iteration (B6, C6, C7)





\((L - \sigma I)\mathbf y = \mathbf x\) for a 2 × 2: \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a\end{pmatrix}\). In code, never form the inverse: factor once and solve. R: F <- Matrix::lu(Matrix::Matrix(M)), then as.vector(solve(F, x)). Python: F = scipy.linalg.lu_factor(M), then scipy.linalg.lu_solve(F, x). Rust: let lu = m.lu(); then lu.solve(&x). RQI changes the shift every step, so there it has to factor every step (solve(A - sigma * diag(n), x)).









Hint 5 — failure checks (C3, C4)





Mod() (R) / np.abs() (Python) of the eigenvalues shows whether two have the same size. power_it returns the iteration count: if it equals maxit, it did not converge. In C4, keep all changes in a vector so you can divide the last one by the one before.

title: Exercise: power iteration and friends
Exercise: power iteration and friends
text:
Where this leads

How eigen() works, and big problems (next unit): eigen() finds all eigenvalues with the QR algorithm, which is, in outline, a clever shifted inverse iteration on all vectors at once. For a few eigenpairs of a huge sparse matrix (the top principal components of a 100 000-cell dataset), Krylov methods (Lanczos, irlba, RSpectra, scipy.sparse.linalg.eigsh) improve on power iteration by keeping all the vectors \(\mathbf x, A\mathbf x, A^2\mathbf x, \dots\) instead of only the last one.
Equilibria, stability and the phase plane (Part 8): the stability of an equilibrium of an ODE model is decided by the eigenvalues of its Jacobian, and the slowest-decaying direction is again an eigenvector.
Stochastic simulation (Part 8): the Markov chains there run in continuous time; their long-run behaviour is again a stationary distribution.
Iterative linear solvers in depth (Part 11): Jacobi and similar methods converge at a rate set by the largest eigenvalue of an iteration matrix, the same \(|\lambda|^k\) argument as in this unit.

title: Quiz: power iteration and friends
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of power iteration, the Rayleigh quotient and inverse iteration. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Power iteration repeats \(\mathbf x \leftarrow A\mathbf x/\|A\mathbf x\|\). What does \(\mathbf x\) converge to, and what two conditions are needed?






Hint





Write \(\mathbf x_0 = c_1\mathbf v_1 + c_2\mathbf v_2 + \dots\) and multiply by \(A\) \(k\) times.









Answer





To the eigenvector \(\mathbf v_1\) of the eigenvalue of largest modulus. Needed: (1) that eigenvalue is strictly dominant, \(|\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2|\); (2) the start has a component along it, \(c_1 \ne 0\). For a nonnegative Leslie or Markov matrix with a nonnegative start, (2) holds automatically, and (1) holds unless the life cycle or chain is periodic.




Q2. For a three-age-class Leslie matrix, eigen() returns \(\lambda_1 = 0.95\) and the first eigenvector \((-0.8, -0.5, -0.3)\). What do these tell a conservation biologist?






Hint





Eigenvectors come with arbitrary length and sign.









Answer





In the long run the population declines by 5 % per year. The stable age distribution is the eigenvector rescaled to sum 1: \((0.8, 0.5, 0.3)/1.6 = (0.50, 0.31, 0.19)\), half of the animals in the youngest class. The minus signs mean nothing: any nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector.




Q3. A matrix has eigenvalues \(2\), \(-1.8\) and \(0.5\). At what rate does power iteration converge, and roughly how many iterations does each decimal digit take? What would you see in the eigenvalue estimates?






Hint





Rate \(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|\); one digit takes \(1/\log_{10}|\lambda_1/\lambda_2|\) steps.









Answer





Rate \(1.8/2 = 0.9\); one digit takes \(1/\log_{10}(1/0.9) \approx 22\) iterations, so about 220 for 10 digits. Because \(\lambda_2\) is negative, the error alternates in sign: the estimates jump above and below \(\lambda_1 = 2\) while closing in on it.




Q4. Why does power iteration normalise \(\mathbf x\) every step? Does the normalisation change what it converges to?






Hint





How large is \(A^k\mathbf x\) after 5000 steps if \(\lambda_1 = 1.2\)? If \(\lambda_1 = 0.5\)?









Answer





\(A^k\mathbf x\) grows or shrinks like \(\lambda_1^k\), so without normalisation it overflows to Inf (then NaN) or underflows to 0. Normalising only rescales: the direction, which is what converges, is the same. Different norms (sum, 2-norm, max) give the same eigenvector with different scaling, and the eigenvalue estimate must be computed to match.




Q5. A biennial plant has \(L = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ 0.25 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\). What do these lines print, and what is wrong?

RPythonRust


L <- matrix(c(0, 4, 0.25, 0), 2, byrow = TRUE)
for (steps in c(100, 101)) {
  x <- c(1, 0)
  for (k in 1:steps) { y <- drop(L %*% x); x <- y / sum(y) }
  cat(steps, x, "\n")
}


import numpy as np

L = np.array([[0, 4], [0.25, 0]])
for steps in [100, 101]:
    x = np.array([1.0, 0])
    for k in range(steps):
        y = L @ x
        x = y / y.sum()
    print(steps, x)


// rust/examples/power_iteration_q5.rs  —  cargo run --example power_iteration_q5
// Q5: power iteration on the biennial plant after 100 and 101 steps.
use nalgebra::{DMatrix, DVector};

fn main() {
    let l = DMatrix::from_row_slice(2, 2, &[0.0, 4.0, 0.25, 0.0]);
    for steps in [100, 101] {
        let mut x = DVector::from_row_slice(&[1.0, 0.0]);
        for _ in 0..steps {
            let y = &l * &x;
            x = &y / y.sum();
        }
        println!("{} {:?}", steps, x.as_slice());
    }
}









Hint





Compute \(L^2\), and the eigenvalues of \(L\).









Answer





After 100 steps \(\mathbf x = (1, 0)\), after 101 steps \((0, 1)\). \(L^2 = I\) and the eigenvalues are \(+1\) and \(-1\): equal modulus, so nothing dominates and the iteration cycles with period 2 forever (rosette year, flowering year). A fixed number of iterations without a convergence check would return either answer. Check the residual \(\|L\mathbf x - \lambda\mathbf x\|\), or look at Mod(eigen(L)$values).




Q6. Why is the largest eigenvalue of a Markov transition matrix always exactly 1? What then sets how fast a simulation of the chain reaches its stationary distribution?






Hint





What is \(P\) times a vector of ones?









Answer





Each row of \(P\) sums to 1, so \(P\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1\): 1 is an eigenvalue of \(P\), and therefore of \(P^T\) (same eigenvalues). No eigenvalue can be larger in modulus, because multiplying by \(P\) cannot increase total probability. The rate is \(|\lambda_2|\): the deviation from \(\boldsymbol\pi\) shrinks by about \(|\lambda_2|\) per step. Biologically, \(|\lambda_2|\) sets the relaxation time of the population after a perturbation such as cell sorting.




Q7. A Markov chain simulation changes by at most \(10^{-9}\) in its last step, and the changes have been shrinking by a factor 0.999 per step. Roughly how far is it from the stationary distribution?






Hint





The remaining error is the sum of all future changes: a geometric series.









Answer





About \(10^{-9}\cdot 0.999/(1 - 0.999) \approx 10^{-6}\), a thousand times the last change. A small change per step is not a small error when the rate is close to 1. Use a residual or a rate-corrected estimate to stop, or speed things up with inverse iteration and a shift just above 1.




Q8. For a symmetric matrix, the current vector \(\mathbf x\) differs from the eigenvector by about \(10^{-4}\). Roughly how accurate is the Rayleigh quotient \(\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x/\mathbf x^T\mathbf x\) as an estimate of \(\lambda_1\)? And for a nonsymmetric matrix?






Hint





For symmetric matrices the eigenvectors are orthogonal, and the first-order error term cancels.









Answer





Symmetric: error of order \((10^{-4})^2 = 10^{-8}\) (times \(|\lambda_1 - \lambda_2|\)), so the eigenvalue has about twice as many correct digits as the vector. Nonsymmetric (e.g. a Leslie matrix): only of order \(10^{-4}\), no gain.




Q9. A matrix has eigenvalues \(5\), \(2\), \(1.9\) and \(0.1\). Which eigenvalue does inverse iteration find with shift \(\sigma = 2.1\), and at what rate? Which shift would you use to find \(0.1\) quickly?






Hint





The eigenvalues of \((A - \sigma I)^{-1}\) are \(1/(\lambda_i - \sigma)\); the rate is (distance to the nearest) / (distance to the next nearest).









Answer





\(\sigma = 2.1\) is nearest to \(2\) (distance 0.1); next nearest is \(1.9\) (distance 0.2). It finds \(\lambda = 2\) at rate \(0.1/0.2 = 0.5\): slow, because 2 and 1.9 are close. A shift closer to 2, such as 2.01, gives \(0.01/0.11 = 0.09\). For \(0.1\): \(\sigma = 0\) (plain inverse iteration) gives rate \(0.1/1.9 = 0.05\); \(\sigma = 0.1\) minus a little does even better.




Q10. In inverse iteration the shift is exactly an eigenvalue, so \(A - \sigma I\) is singular, or nearly so after rounding. Is the computed eigenvector then useless?






Hint





In which direction is the huge, inaccurate solution \(\mathbf y\) of \((A - \sigma I)\mathbf y = \mathbf x\) pointing?









Answer





No. The solution is huge and its size is meaningless, but it points almost exactly along the eigenvector, because \((A - \sigma I)^{-1}\) magnifies that direction by far more than any other. After normalising, one step gives nearly full precision (the cell-state chain with \(\sigma = 1 + 10^{-15}\): 14 digits). The only practical problem is that some solvers (R’s solve) refuse an exactly singular matrix; nudge the shift slightly.




Q11. Inverse iteration on a \(2000 \times 2000\) dense matrix takes 30 steps. Compare the work of calling solve(A - sigma * I, x) in every step with factoring once and reusing the factors.






Hint





LU costs about \(\tfrac23 n^3\); forward plus back substitution about \(2n^2\).









Answer





solve every step: \(30\cdot\tfrac23\cdot 2000^3 \approx 1.6\times10^{11}\) operations. Factor once: \(\tfrac23\cdot 2000^3 \approx 5.3\times10^9\) plus \(30\cdot 2\cdot 2000^2 = 2.4\times10^8\) for the solves, about 30 times less. (Rayleigh quotient iteration changes the shift every step and so must refactor every step; it makes up for it by needing only 2–3 steps.)




Q12. When would you write power iteration yourself instead of calling eigen()?






Hint





What does eigen() compute, and what does it cost in time and memory?









Answer





eigen() computes all eigenvalues with \(O(n^3)\) work and \(n^2\) memory: the right choice for any matrix you can hold dense (a 4 × 4 Leslie matrix, a 500-state chain). Power or inverse iteration is worth it when you need only one eigenpair of a large or sparse matrix, such as the growth rate of a size-structured model with thousands of classes, or the stationary distribution of a sparse chain with \(10^6\) states, where each step is one cheap (sparse) matrix–vector product or solve. And it is already what you do when you simulate the model forward.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
About this lecture
A population model that is run forward year after year computes, without being asked, the dominant eigenvalue and eigenvector of its matrix. This lecture turns that observation into an algorithm and asks when it works.

Power iteration: multiply by A again and again, and normalise. The direction settles on the dominant eigenvector, the scale factor on the dominant eigenvalue.
Convergence rate |\lambda_2/\lambda_1|: linear convergence, fast or hopelessly slow depending on the second eigenvalue. It fails when |\lambda_2| = |\lambda_1|.
Rayleigh quotient: a better eigenvalue estimate from the same vector (twice the digits for symmetric matrices).
Inverse iteration and shifts: iterate with (A - \sigma I)^{-1} to find the eigenvalue nearest \sigma, in a few steps.
Biology: a Leslie matrix (long-term growth rate and stable age distribution of a fish population) and the stationary distribution of a Markov chain of cell states.


This opens Part 5. Students have met eigenvalues in a first linear algebra course (characteristic polynomial of a 2 x 2), and the svd unit used eigen() in passing. Here we build the simplest eigenvalue algorithm by hand, in ten lines, the way the course builds every method first. The point that makes this unit easy to motivate: ecologists projecting a Leslie matrix and biologists simulating a Markov chain are already running power iteration. The numerical analysis is about how fast it converges, how to tell when it has, and what to do when it is too slow. How eigen() itself works (the QR algorithm) and Krylov methods for large problems are the next unit, How eigen() works, and big problems.

title: Power iteration and friends
section: A biology problem: a stocked lake
text:
A biology problem: a stocked lake
A lake is stocked with 1000 one-year-old fish. Each year, fish of age i survive to age i+1 with probability s_i, and produce F_i offspring that are counted next year as age 0.


After a few wobbly years every age class grows by the same factor, about 1.177 per year.
The proportions in the age classes settle at 69 %, 18 %, 9 %, 4 %, whatever the starting stock.
What are these two numbers, how fast are they reached, and when are they not reached at all?


Start with the picture, not the algebra. Left: numbers per age class on a log scale; after about ten years all four lines are parallel straight lines, so each class grows by the same factor every year. Right: the proportions, with wild swings in the first years (the stocked cohort moving through the age classes) that die out. Fisheries and conservation biologists want exactly these two numbers: the long-term growth rate lambda (is the population viable? lambda > 1 grows) and the stable age distribution (what a survey at equilibrium should find). They also care about the transient: how long until the wobbles are gone. All three are eigen-questions.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
The Leslie matrix
Write the numbers in age classes 0–3 as a vector \mathbf n_t. One year later, \mathbf n_{t+1} = L\,\mathbf n_t:

L = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1.5 & 4 & 5 \\ 0.3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.5 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\quad \begin{array}{l} \leftarrow \text{offspring } F_i \text{ per fish of age } i \\ \leftarrow \text{survival } s_0 \\ \leftarrow s_1 \\ \leftarrow s_2 \end{array}

L <- matrix(0, 4, 4)
L[1, ] <- c(0, 1.5, 4, 5)                  # offspring per fish of each age
L[cbind(2:4, 1:3)] <- c(0.3, 0.6, 0.5)     # survival to the next age
n <- c(0, 1000, 0, 0)                      # stock 1000 one-year-olds
for (t in 1:30) n <- L %*% n
round(drop(n))
# [1] 180810  46072  23479   9971
sum(L %*% n) / sum(n)                      # growth of the total in year 31
# [1] 1.177361

A Leslie matrix (P. H. Leslie, 1945) has fertilities in the first row and survival probabilities on the subdiagonal, zeros elsewhere. Read row 1: next year’s age-0 fish are 1.5 per one-year-old plus 4 per two-year-old plus 5 per three-year-old. Rows 2-4: the survivors move one class down. Nobody survives past age 3. %*% is R’s matrix product; drop() turns the 4 x 1 matrix back into a vector. The numbers are made up but of a realistic shape for a short-lived fish. The same structure, with hundreds of size classes instead of four ages, is an integral projection model; we come back to that at the end.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Recap: eigenvalues of a 2 × 2
A two-age-class plant: L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0.75 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. An eigenvector \mathbf v \ne \mathbf 0 satisfies L\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v; the eigenvalues solve \det(L - \lambda I) = 0:
\det\begin{pmatrix} 1-\lambda & 1 \\ 0.75 & -\lambda \end{pmatrix} = \lambda^2 - \lambda - 0.75 = (\lambda - 1.5)(\lambda + 0.5) = 0









\lambda_1 = 1.5
\lambda_2 = -0.5




solve (L - \lambda I)\mathbf v = \mathbf 0
-0.5v_1 + v_2 = 0
1.5v_1 + v_2 = 0


eigenvector
\mathbf v_1 = (2, 1)
\mathbf v_2 = (2, -3)


check
L\mathbf v_1 = (3, 1.5) = 1.5\,\mathbf v_1
L\mathbf v_2 = (-1, 1.5) = -0.5\,\mathbf v_2




Biology: the population grows by 1.5 per year in the long run, with juveniles : adults = 2 : 1 (67 % juveniles).
Any multiple of \mathbf v is also an eigenvector: we choose the scaling (here, proportions summing to 1).


One-slide recap of first-course linear algebra. The characteristic polynomial works for 2 x 2 and 3 x 3 by hand; for 4 x 4 and up it is no longer how anyone computes eigenvalues (and finding roots of a high-degree polynomial is badly conditioned anyway, see How eigen() works, and big problems). Keep this matrix: we use it on the next slide to see why repeated multiplication finds lambda_1, and in the exercise by hand. Note lambda_2 is negative: the second eigenvector has a negative entry, so it is not a population, only a pattern of deviations.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Why repeated multiplication finds \lambda_1
Write the start as a combination of eigenvectors: \mathbf x_0 = (1, 0) = \tfrac38(2, 1) + \tfrac18(2, -3). Each multiplication by L multiplies each part by its own eigenvalue:
L^k\mathbf x_0 = \tfrac38\,(1.5)^k\,(2, 1) + \tfrac18\,(-0.5)^k\,(2, -3) \;=\; (1.5)^k\Big[\tfrac38(2,1) + \tfrac18\big(-\tfrac13\big)^k(2,-3)\Big]



k
L^k\mathbf x_0
total ratio
error in \lambda




1
(1, 0.75)
1.75
+0.25


2
(1.75, 0.75)
1.4286
-0.071


3
(2.5, 1.3125)
1.525
+0.025


4
(3.8125, 1.875)
