The \mathbf v_2 part shrinks relative to the \mathbf v_1 part by |\lambda_2/\lambda_1| = \tfrac13 per step; the error shrinks by about 3 per step and flips sign (because \lambda_2 < 0).
This needs |\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2| and a start with some \mathbf v_1 in it.


This is the whole theory of the power method in one 2 x 2 example. “Total ratio” is sum(L^k x0) / sum(L^(k-1) x0), the growth factor of the total population. Its error alternates in sign because (-1/3)^k alternates. For an n x n matrix with n independent eigenvectors the same argument gives L^k x0 = sum c_i lambda_i^k v_i, dominated by the largest |lambda_i| as long as c_1 is not 0. For a nonnegative Leslie or Markov matrix any nonnegative, nonzero start has c_1 > 0, so the condition is automatic there.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Power iteration
Repeat:

\mathbf y = A\mathbf x_k (one matrix–vector product, 2n^2 operations)
eigenvalue estimate \lambda^{(k)} from \mathbf x_k and \mathbf y
normalise: \mathbf x_{k+1} = \mathbf y / \|\mathbf y\|

Why normalise? A^k\mathbf x grows or shrinks like \lambda_1^k. For the fish (\lambda_1 = 1.18):
x <- c(0, 1, 0, 0)
for (k in 1:5000) x <- L %*% x             # no normalisation
drop(x)
# [1] NaN NaN NaN NaN                      # 1.18^5000 overflows, then Inf - Inf
x <- c(0, 1, 0, 0)
for (k in 1:5000) x <- (0.5 * L) %*% x     # a declining population
drop(x)
# [1] 0 0 0 0                              # underflow
For a nonnegative matrix (Leslie, Markov) the natural norm is the sum: \mathbf x holds proportions, and \lambda^{(k)} = \mathrm{sum}(A\mathbf x_k) is the growth of the total.

Normalising does not change the direction, only the length, and the direction is what converges. Overflow needs about 709.8 / log(1.177) = 4346 steps here, so it is not the first problem a student hits, but a population with lambda = 3 overflows after 650 steps and a large matrix with lambda_1 = 1000 after about 100. The NaN comes from Inf * 0 in the matrix product (the zeros of L times infinite entries). Any norm will do: the 2-norm is the default for general matrices (next slides), the max-norm is common in textbooks, the sum is natural when all entries are nonnegative. Each gives the same direction, scaled differently.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Power iteration in R
power_it <- function(A, x, tol = 1e-10, maxit = 1000) {
  x <- x / sum(x)
  for (k in 1:maxit) {
    y <- drop(A %*% x)
    lambda <- sum(y)                     # growth factor of the total
    r <- sqrt(sum((y - lambda * x)^2))   # residual ||Ax - lambda x||
    x <- y / lambda                      # normalise: proportions
    if (r < tol) break
  }
  list(lambda = lambda, x = x, k = k, r = r)
}

Stop on the residual \|A\mathbf x - \lambda\mathbf x\|: it is zero exactly for an eigenpair, and it is cheap (we have A\mathbf x already).
Always return the iteration count and the residual, so the caller can see whether it converged.


Ten lines, one matrix-vector product per step. drop() turns the one-column matrix from %*% into a plain vector. The residual uses the old x and the new y, so it costs nothing extra. Why the residual and not the change between iterates: we will see a case where the change is tiny and the answer is still wrong. The convergence check matters more than usual here, because power iteration can fail silently (two slides on).

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
How fast? |\lambda_2 / \lambda_1| per step


The fish: |\lambda_2/\lambda_1| = 0.770/1.177 = 0.654. Linear convergence: the error falls by 0.654 per step, a slope of \log_{10} 0.654 = -0.18: about 5.4 steps per digit, 55 steps for 10^{-10}.
\lambda_2 is complex here, so the error wiggles (the transient oscillation in the age distribution), but the envelope is |\lambda_2/\lambda_1|^k.
Biology: \lambda_1/|\lambda_2| = 1.53 is the damping ratio: how fast a population forgets its initial age structure.


Error against iteration on a log scale, as for every iterative method in the course (Convergence and cost). The dashed line has the predicted slope; both errors follow it. Note the eigenvalue error and the eigenvector error converge at the same rate here; that changes for symmetric matrices (Rayleigh quotient, later). The rate comes straight from the 2 x 2 argument: the second-largest term shrinks by lambda_2/lambda_1 relative to the first. Ecologists use the damping ratio rho = lambda_1/|lambda_2| (Caswell, Matrix Population Models) to say how long transients last: the distance to the stable age distribution falls like rho^(-t). The same number is the convergence rate of the numerical method: as in Bisection and fixed-point iteration, “the population settles” and “the iteration converges” are the same statement.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
When it fails: |\lambda_2| = |\lambda_1|
A salmon-like fish that spawns once, at age 3, and dies: first row (0, 0, 0, 12).

Ls <- L;  Ls[1, ] <- c(0, 0, 0, 12)        # spawn once at age 3, then die
Mod(eigen(Ls)$values)                      # Mod = |lambda|
# [1] 1.019427 1.019427 1.019427 1.019427
out <- power_it(Ls, c(0, 1, 0, 0), maxit = 200);  c(out$k, out$r)
# [1] 200.0000000   0.4242641                # hit maxit; residual not small

Four eigenvalues of equal modulus, lambda^4 = 12 x 0.3 x 0.6 x 0.5 = 1.08, spread evenly around a circle. No eigenvalue dominates, so nothing converges: the estimate cycles 0.6, 0.5, 12, 0.3 forever, because the stocked cohort only reproduces every fourth year. This is real biology: pink salmon live exactly two years, and odd-year and even-year runs in the same river are separate populations with different sizes; periodical cicadas emerge every 13 or 17 years. Mathematically the matrix is “imprimitive” (Perron-Frobenius theorem: a nonnegative matrix is guaranteed a strictly dominant positive eigenvalue only if some power of it has all entries positive). The check: the residual does not fall, and maxit is reached. Never return the last estimate without that check. The long-run growth over a full cycle is still well defined: lambda^4 = 1.08 per four years.

title: Power iteration and friends
section: A Markov chain of cell states
text:
A Markov chain of cell states
Cancer cells switch between stem-like (S), basal (B) and luminal (L) states. Row i of P holds the probabilities that a cell in state i is in each state one day later:


P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.80 & 0.15 & 0.05 \\ 0.05 & 0.90 & 0.05 \\ 0.05 & 0.10 & 0.85 \end{pmatrix}

Rows sum to 1.
Proportions \mathbf p (a row vector): \mathbf p_{t+1} = \mathbf p_t P.
Stationary distribution: \boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi, i.e. P^T\boldsymbol\pi^T = 1\cdot\boldsymbol\pi^T: an eigenvector of P^T with \lambda = 1.




Sorting any one state and letting it grow gives the same equilibrium mix (dashed): 20 % S, 55 % B, 25 % L.

This is the “phenotypic equilibrium” of Gupta et al. (2011, Cell): breast cancer cell lines sorted into stem-like, basal and luminal subpopulations each regenerated the original mix within days, and a three-state Markov chain explained it. Our P is illustrative, not their fitted matrix. The largest eigenvalue of a stochastic matrix is exactly 1 (P times the ones vector is the ones vector, so 1 is an eigenvalue of P and hence of P^T), and for a chain where every state can reach every other and the chain is not periodic, all other eigenvalues have modulus < 1. Same Perron-Frobenius story as the Leslie matrix. R convention: p is a row vector and we multiply p %*% P; that is power iteration with P^T.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Power iteration on the chain
Simulating the cell population is power iteration. The sum stays 1, so no normalisation is needed.
P <- matrix(c(0.80, 0.15, 0.05,
              0.05, 0.90, 0.05,
              0.05, 0.10, 0.85), 3, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(c("S", "B", "L"), c("S", "B", "L")))
p <- c(1, 0, 0)                            # start: sorted stem-like cells
for (day in 1:60) p <- p %*% P
round(p, 6)
#        S    B    L
# [1,] 0.2 0.55 0.25
eigen(t(P))$values
# [1] 1.00 0.80 0.75

Rate |\lambda_2/\lambda_1| = 0.8: about 10 steps per digit; the deviation from equilibrium halves every 3.1 days (\log 0.5/\log 0.8).
So \lambda_2 is a biological quantity too: the relaxation time of the cell population after a perturbation.


For a Markov chain lambda_1 = 1 is known, so the rate is just |lambda_2|. 0.8^60 = 1.5e-6, enough for 6 printed digits. 1/log10(1/0.8) = 10.3 steps per digit. The relaxation time is what you would measure in the sorting experiment: how many days until the mix is back within 1 % of equilibrium (log 0.01 / log 0.8 = 20.6 days). Note t(P): R’s eigen gives right eigenvectors (columns), so the stationary distribution is an eigenvector of the transpose. Python users: np.linalg.eig(P.T).

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
When it fails: slow switching
A second cell line switches state 100 times less often: P_\text{slow} = I + 0.01\,(P - I). Same \boldsymbol\pi, but \lambda_2 = 0.998.


Pslow <- diag(3) + 0.01 * (P - diag(3))
p <- c(1, 0, 0)
for (k in 1:1e5) {
  p_new <- drop(p %*% Pslow)
  change <- max(abs(p_new - p))
  p <- p_new
  if (change < 1e-8) break
}
k;  change
# [1] 5406
# [1] 9.989544e-09
max(abs(p - c(0.2, 0.55, 0.25)))
# [1] 4.984782e-06           # 500 x tol




Each step moves by only (1 - \lambda_2) = 0.002 times the remaining error, so a small change is not a small error: error \approx change \cdot\,\lambda_2/(1-\lambda_2) = change \times 500.
Check: estimate \lambda_2 from the ratio of successive changes; if it is near 1, distrust the stopping rule (and use the red line: inverse iteration, coming up).


This is the classic false convergence of a slowly converging linear iteration, the same as in Bisection and fixed-point iteration when |g’| is close to 1. 5406 iterations, and still only 5 correct digits, while the stopping rule claims 8. The geometric series argument: if each step’s change is c times the previous, the remaining error is change x c/(1-c). The ratio of successive changes is a cheap estimate of c. Biologically, rare switching is common (epigenetic states that persist for many divisions), and a Markov model of it is exactly this kind of nearly-decomposable, slowly mixing chain. The orange line in the figure (the change) is 500 times below the blue line (the error) the whole time.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
The Rayleigh quotient
For any nonzero \mathbf x, the best single number \lambda with A\mathbf x \approx \lambda\mathbf x (least squares) is the Rayleigh quotient
R(\mathbf x) = \frac{\mathbf x^T A\mathbf x}{\mathbf x^T\mathbf x}, \qquad R(\mathbf v) = \lambda \text{ exactly for an eigenvector } \mathbf v.
General power iteration (any real matrix): 2-norm, Rayleigh quotient as the estimate.
power_rq <- function(A, x, tol = 1e-10, maxit = 1000) {
  x <- x / sqrt(sum(x^2))
  for (k in 1:maxit) {
    y <- drop(A %*% x)
    lambda <- sum(x * y)                 # Rayleigh quotient (x has length 1)
    r <- sqrt(sum((y - lambda * x)^2))   # residual
    x <- y / sqrt(sum(y^2))
    if (r < tol) break
  }
  list(lambda = lambda, x = x, k = k, r = r)
}

Where the formula comes from: minimise ||Ax - lambda x||^2 over the single number lambda; this is least squares with one column x and right-hand side Ax (Least squares: normal equations vs QR), and the normal equation is x^T x lambda = x^T A x. Unlike the sum, it works for matrices with negative entries and negative eigenvalues, and it carries the sign of lambda. sum(x * y) is the dot product x^T y; crossprod(x, y) does the same. This version is what a textbook calls “the” power method.

title: Power iteration and friends
section: Rayleigh quotient: twice the digits for symmetric A
text:
Rayleigh quotient: twice the digits for symmetric A


Left: correlation matrix of three fish traits (\lambda = 1.607, 0.811, 0.581; ratio 0.505). If \mathbf x is off by \delta, R(\mathbf x) is off by about \delta^2: the eigenvalue converges like |\lambda_2/\lambda_1|^{2k}, the vector still like |\lambda_2/\lambda_1|^{k}.
Right: for the (nonsymmetric) Leslie matrix there is no gain.


For symmetric A the eigenvectors are orthogonal, so with x = v1 + delta v2 (unit eigenvectors), R(x) = (lambda1 + delta^2 lambda2)/(1 + delta^2) = lambda1 - delta^2 (lambda1 - lambda2) + …: the first-order term cancels. For nonsymmetric matrices the eigenvectors are not orthogonal and the cross term survives, so the error stays first order. The correlation matrix is C = (1, .4, .3; .4, 1, .2; .3, .2, 1) for body length, body depth and fin length (made up). Its leading eigenvector (0.63, 0.58, 0.51) is the overall “size” axis: the first principal component, which is where How eigen() works, and big problems starts. The flat dots at 1e-16 on the left are rounding: the Rayleigh quotient has reached machine precision after 25 steps while the sum ratio needs about 50.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Inverse iteration
If A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v, then (A - \sigma I)^{-1}\mathbf v = \dfrac{1}{\lambda - \sigma}\,\mathbf v: same eigenvectors, eigenvalues 1/(\lambda_i - \sigma).
The eigenvalue closest to the shift \sigma becomes the largest. Power iteration on (A - \sigma I)^{-1} finds it, at rate
\frac{|\lambda_\text{nearest} - \sigma|}{|\lambda_\text{next nearest} - \sigma|}
The 2 × 2 plant (\lambda = 1.5, -0.5):









shift \sigma
eigenvalues of (L - \sigma I)^{-1}
finds

—

0.5/1.5 = 0.33


\sigma = 1.4
1/0.1 = 10, \ 1/(-1.9) = -0.53

1/1.5 = 0.67, \ 1/(-0.5) = -2

\sigma = -0.4
1/1.9 = 0.53, \ 1/(-0.1) = -10
-0.5
0.1/1.9 = 0.053




Two ideas in one. Inverting turns smallest into largest; shifting moves which eigenvalue is “smallest”. A good shift (close to the eigenvalue you want, far from the others) gives a rate near 0: a few iterations suffice. We never form the inverse (Gaussian elimination as LU: never solve(A) %*% b); each step solves a linear system (A - sigma I) y = x. sigma = 0 is plain inverse iteration and finds the eigenvalue of smallest modulus. Which eigenvalue you get depends only on the shift, not on which one you wanted: that is the failure mode we see two slides on.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Inverse iteration in R
inv_it <- function(A, sigma, x, tol = 1e-12, maxit = 100) {
  M <- A - sigma * diag(nrow(A))
  for (k in 1:maxit) {
    y <- solve(M, x)                       # one linear solve per step
    x <- y / sqrt(sum(y^2))
    Ax <- drop(A %*% x)
    lambda <- sum(x * Ax)                  # Rayleigh quotient with A itself
    r <- sqrt(sum((Ax - lambda * x)^2))
    if (r < tol) break
  }
  list(lambda = lambda, x = x, k = k, r = r)
}

Each step is a solve with the same matrix: factor once (\tfrac23 n^3), then each step costs only 2n^2 (forward and back substitution). In R: Matrix::lu; here solve refactors each time, which is fine for n = 3.
The eigenvalue is read off with the Rayleigh quotient of A, not of (A-\sigma I)^{-1}.


Same skeleton as power_rq; the only change is solve(M, x) instead of A %*% x. Factor once, solve many times is the lesson of Gaussian elimination as LU; for an n = 2000 matrix that is the difference between 5e9 operations per step and 8e6. Python: scipy.linalg.lu_factor once, lu_solve each step. We could also get lambda from the growth factor mu of the inverse iteration (lambda = sigma + 1/mu), but the Rayleigh quotient of A is simpler and does not need to track the sign.

title: Power iteration and friends
section: A shift near 1 fixes the slow chain
text:
A shift near 1 fixes the slow chain
We know \lambda_1 = 1 for a Markov chain, so shift just above it: rate \approx 10^{-6}/0.002 = 5\times10^{-4}.
out <- inv_it(t(Pslow), sigma = 1 + 1e-6, x = c(1, 0, 0))
out$k
# [1] 3
print(out$x / sum(out$x), digits = 15)
#                 S                 B                 L
# 0.200000000051137 0.549999999980061 0.249999999968802









iteration
1
2
3




error, inverse iteration
3.2\times10^{-4}
1.3\times10^{-7}
5.1\times10^{-11}


error, power iteration
0.80
0.80
0.80 (still 5\times10^{-6} after 5406 steps)



Each step gains \log_{10}(1/5\times10^{-4}) \approx 3.3 digits.

Three linear solves against 5406 matrix-vector products, and the answer is better. Rescale to proportions at the end (x / sum(x)), because inverse iteration normalises in the 2-norm. The table is the red line in the slow-chain figure. This is how stationary distributions of large chains are computed in practice when the chain mixes slowly; for huge sparse chains the solve itself is done iteratively, but the idea is the same.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Shift exactly at the eigenvalue?
A - \lambda I is singular when \lambda is an eigenvalue. Is that a problem?
solve(t(P) - diag(3), c(1, 0, 0))          # shift exactly 1
# Error: system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number = 3.46945e-17
y <- solve(t(P) - (1 + 1e-15) * diag(3), c(1, 0, 0))
y
#             S             B             L
# -1.847631e+14 -5.080984e+14 -2.309538e+14
print(y / sum(y), digits = 15)
#                 S                 B                 L
# 0.200000000000003 0.549999999999998 0.249999999999999

\kappa \approx 10^{16}, so \mathbf y is huge and inaccurate, but the error lies almost entirely along the eigenvector, which is what we want. One step, 14 digits.
R’s solve refuses an exactly singular matrix; nudge the shift by a tiny amount.


This surprises everyone who has learnt “never solve an ill-conditioned system” (Pivoting, norms and conditioning). The huge solution is exactly what we want: (A - sigma I)^{-1} has one eigenvalue of size 1e15 and the others of size 5-10, so whatever the rounding errors, the result points along the eigenvector. Normalisation throws the size away. numpy’s solve does not check the condition number and returns a huge vector for the exact shift as well; R checks rcond against machine epsilon and stops. Do not use this argument for linear systems in general: it works here only because we want the direction, not the vector.

title: Power iteration and friends
section: Other eigenvalues: shift near the one you want
text:
Other eigenvalues: shift near the one you want
\lambda_2 of the cell-state chain sets the relaxation time. Shift near it:
o <- inv_it(t(P), sigma = 0.82, x = c(1, 0, 0));  o$k;  o$lambda;  round(o$x, 4)
# [1] 21
# [1] 0.8
#       S       B       L
#  0.0000 -0.7071  0.7071
o <- inv_it(t(P), sigma = 0.77, x = c(1, 0, 0));  o$k;  o$lambda
# [1] 58
# [1] 0.75                                   # not the one we wanted!

The slowest deviation from equilibrium is an exchange between B and L (sums to 0: not a population, a pattern).
Failure: the shift picks the nearest eigenvalue. 0.77 is nearer to 0.75 than to 0.8. With close eigenvalues the rate is poor (here 0.29 and 0.67).
Check: for a small matrix, compare with eigen(); for a big one, try several shifts and see which eigenvalues you get.


The eigenvector of P^T for lambda = 0.8 is (0, -1, 1)/sqrt(2): starting from any mix, the last deviation to disappear is a surplus of basal cells balanced by a deficit of luminal ones (or vice versa). That is a biological prediction: if you sort a population that is too luminal, it relaxes more slowly than one that is too stem-like (lambda_3 = 0.75, eigenvector (1, -1, 0)). Rates: |0.8 - 0.82| / |0.75 - 0.82| = 0.29 and |0.75 - 0.77| / |0.8 - 0.77| = 0.67, which match 21 and 58 iterations to 1e-12. Finding several eigenvalues reliably is what deflation and the QR algorithm do (next unit).

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Rayleigh quotient iteration
Use the current Rayleigh quotient as the shift, updated every step. Trait correlation matrix C, start (1, 1, 1):



step
shift \sigma_k = R(\mathbf x_k)

For symmetric A the error is cubed each step (0.08 → 7\times10^{-4} → 4\times10^{-10}); full precision in 2–3 steps.
Costs a new factorisation every step (\tfrac23 n^3 each).
Failure: start (1, 0, 0) converges, just as fast, to \lambda_2 = 0.8113: RQI finds the eigenvalue nearest the start, not the largest.
One more step and C - \sigma I is singular to machine precision: R’s solve stops with an error. Stop on the residual first.


Rayleigh quotient iteration combines the two ideas of the lecture: the Rayleigh quotient is the best eigenvalue estimate, and a shift at the best estimate gives the fastest inverse iteration. For symmetric matrices the convergence is cubic, faster than Newton’s quadratic convergence (Newton and secant methods). For nonsymmetric matrices it is quadratic. The price is a factorisation per step, which is why it is used for refinement of a few eigenpairs, not as a general method. The QR algorithm inside eigen() uses shifts chosen in much the same spirit (next unit). The code is in the exercise (C7).

text:
Power iteration or eigen()?

For a matrix you can hold dense, eigen() is the default. Write power iteration when you need one eigenpair of a big or sparse matrix, or when the iteration is the model.

The n = 2000 row is an integral projection model (IPM): a Leslie-type matrix over 2000 body-size classes, with growth spreading each class over its neighbours. Timings from one run on a multi-core desktop; your numbers will differ, the ratio will not by much. eigen() computes 2000 complex eigenvalues, power iteration needed 40 steps because this IPM has |lambda_2/lambda_1| = 0.63. Sparse chains of 10^6 states (gene-regulatory state spaces, PageRank-like problems on cell-cell graphs) cannot be stored dense at all. The professional tools for a few eigenpairs of huge matrices (Arnoldi/Lanczos: RSpectra, irlba, scipy.sparse.linalg.eigs) start from the same idea and are the topic of How eigen() works, and big problems.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Checklist: eigenvalues by iteration

No convergence after maxit, estimates cycling → |\lambda_2| = |\lambda_1| (periodic life cycle, imprimitive matrix). Check Mod(eigen(A)$values) on a small version.
Slow convergence → estimate the rate from successive changes; true error \approx change \cdot\,c/(1-c). Use a shift and inverse iteration.
Stop on the residual \|A\mathbf x - \lambda\mathbf x\|, never only on the change.
Normalise every step (sum for proportions, 2-norm otherwise), or \lambda^k overflows.
Inverse iteration returned an unexpected eigenvalue → it found the one nearest the shift.
Interpret eigenvectors after rescaling: eigen() returns unit length with an arbitrary sign.


Each line is a failure from this lecture with its check. In biology the first two are the common ones: periodic life cycles and rare transitions between states. The last is the most common mistake in practice: reading a stable age distribution of (-0.96, -0.24, …) straight from eigen() and wondering about the minus signs.

title: Power iteration and friends
text:
Summary

Repeated multiplication \mathbf x \leftarrow A\mathbf x / \|A\mathbf x\| converges to the dominant eigenvector; projecting a population or simulating a Markov chain is exactly this.
Leslie matrix: \lambda_1 = long-term growth rate, \mathbf v_1 = stable age distribution. Markov chain: \lambda_1 = 1, eigenvector of P^T = stationary distribution.
Error falls by |\lambda_2/\lambda_1| per step (linear convergence): \lambda_2 is also the biology of transients (damping ratio, relaxation time).
Fails when |\lambda_2| = |\lambda_1|; crawls when the ratio is near 1, and a small change per step is then not a small error. Stop on the residual.
Rayleigh quotient \mathbf x^TA\mathbf x/\mathbf x^T\mathbf x: best eigenvalue estimate; error \delta^2 for symmetric A.
Inverse iteration with shift \sigma: finds the eigenvalue nearest \sigma at rate |\lambda - \sigma|/|\lambda' - \sigma|; factor once. A shift at the eigenvalue is fine.

Next: How eigen() works, and big problems: all eigenvalues at once (the QR algorithm), and a few eigenvalues of a huge sparse matrix (PCA of 100 000 cells).

Two biological matrices, one algorithm, three improvements (Rayleigh quotient, shift, inverse) and two failures (equal moduli, slow convergence). The next unit explains what eigen() does internally, why symmetric problems are easier and better conditioned than nonsymmetric ones, and how Krylov methods (Lanczos, irlba) find the top principal components of a cell x gene matrix without ever forming the covariance matrix.

title: Splines
text:
About this lecture
One polynomial through many points wiggles (Polynomial interpolation). The cure is to use many small pieces, joined smoothly.

Piecewise linear: join the dots. Simple, safe, error O(h^2), but the slope jumps at every point.
Cubic splines: a cubic on each interval, with value, slope and curvature continuous. Finding them means solving a tridiagonal system, O(n).
Boundary conditions (natural, not-a-knot, clamped) decide the two missing equations, and R and Python use different defaults.
Smoothing splines do not pass through noisy data. A penalty \lambda trades bias against noise; GCV chooses \lambda from the data.
Biology: a gene’s expression along a time course or pseudotime; the growth rate as the slope of a smoothed OD curve.


This is the practical interpolation unit: splines are what interp1, splinefun, CubicSpline, geom_smooth, and pseudotime trend fitting in single-cell packages use. The previous unit showed why one high-degree polynomial is a bad idea; here we go local. The second half moves from interpolation (pass through the points) to smoothing (do not), which is what you need with real, noisy measurements. The running example is the logistic OD curve from Convergence and cost, now with measurement noise.

title: Splines
text:
A biology problem first
A plate reader measures OD every 15 min. We want the growth rate N'(t), e.g. its maximum.

cd <- (y[3:n] - y[1:(n - 2)]) / 0.5     # central differences, h = 0.25 h
range(cd)                                # true rate lies between 0.04 and 0.24
# [1] -0.032  0.278
The OD looks clean (noise sd 0.01), but its differences are noisy: a negative growth rate in stationary phase.

Same logistic curve as in Convergence and cost: K = 1.2, N0 = 0.05, r = 0.8 per hour, now sampled every 15 minutes with plate-reader noise of sd 0.01, rounded to 3 decimals. In Convergence and cost the only noise was rounding, 1e-16, and the trouble started at h = 1e-8. Here the noise is 1e-2, so it starts at ordinary step sizes. The central difference divides a difference of two noisy numbers by 2h = 0.5: noise sd of the estimate is sqrt(2) * 0.01 / 0.5 = 0.028, about 12 % of the maximum rate. Making h smaller makes it worse, not better. Numerical differentiation (Part 7) treats the finite-difference side; here we fit a smooth curve first and differentiate the curve.

title: Splines
section: Recap: one polynomial through all points
text:
Recap: one polynomial through all points


8 time points after stimulation of an immediate-early gene. The degree-7 polynomial through them swings down to -3\times10^5 between the points.
Piecewise methods only look at nearby points: a peak at 0.5 h does not disturb the curve at 12 h.


Recap of Polynomial interpolation in one picture. The data: expression in TPM of a gene that spikes 30 minutes after stimulation and returns to baseline, sampled at uneven times, which is typical for time courses (dense early, sparse late). The polynomial goes through every point but is useless in between, the Runge phenomenon on uneven points. Piecewise linear (green) and the cubic spline (blue) stay near the data. Note the blue curve dips below zero near 3 hours; that is a failure we come back to.

title: Splines
text:
Piecewise linear interpolation
On [x_i, x_{i+1}], with h = x_{i+1} - x_i, draw the straight line: p(x) = y_i + \frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{h}\,(x - x_i), \qquad |f(x) - p(x)| \le \frac{h^2}{8}\max |f''|
K <- 1.2; N0 <- 0.05; r <- 0.8
od <- function(t) K / (1 + (K / N0 - 1) * exp(-r * t))
approx(c(2, 3), od(c(2, 3)), xout = 2.5)$y      # line between t = 2 and t = 3
# [1] 0.3007089
od(2.5)                                          # true value
# [1] 0.2917783

Error 0.0089. Bound: h = 1, \max|N''| = 0.0739 on [2, 3], so \tfrac18 \cdot 0.0739 = 0.0092. Halve h → error \div 4: order 2.
approx never overshoots: p always stays between neighbouring data values.
But the slope jumps at every data point. The derivative of a piecewise linear curve is a staircase.


The bound comes from the same Taylor argument as the polynomial interpolation error with two points: (x - x_i)(x - x_{i+1}) f’‘/2, and the product is largest, h^2/4, in the middle. Here the bound is nearly reached because N’’ is close to its maximum on this interval. Piecewise linear is the right default when you only need values and cannot afford surprises: it is what approx, np.interp, and plotting with lines do. But for a growth rate we need the slope, and the slope of a piecewise linear interpolant is just the forward difference on each interval: we are back to finite differences.

title: Splines
section: Cubic splines: what we ask for
text:
Cubic splines: what we ask for
A cubic spline S through (x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n): on each of the n - 1 intervals a cubic, such that

S(x_i) = y_i (passes through the data),
S, S' and S'' are continuous at the interior points x_2, \dots, x_{n-1} (no kinks, no jumps in curvature).

Counting. n - 1 cubics × 4 coefficients = 4n - 4 unknowns.



condition
number




each cubic hits both its end points
2(n-1)


S' continuous at interior points
n - 2


S'' continuous at interior points
n - 2


total
4n - 6



Two conditions are missing. They come from the ends: the boundary conditions.

A cubic is the lowest degree that can match value, slope and curvature on both sides. The name comes from the draughtsman’s spline: a thin flexible strip held by weights at the data points. A strip bends to minimise its bending energy, roughly the integral of the curvature squared, and the natural cubic spline is exactly the curve that minimises the integral of S’’ squared among all smooth curves through the points. That fact comes back with smoothing splines. The two missing conditions are a free choice; different choices give different splines, different near the ends.

title: Splines
text:
Unknowns: the curvatures M_i = S''(x_i)
S'' is linear on each interval (a cubic has a linear second derivative). With A = \dfrac{x_{i+1} - x}{h_i}, B = \dfrac{x - x_i}{h_i}, h_i = x_{i+1} - x_i:
S(x) = A\,y_i + B\,y_{i+1} + \frac{h_i^2}{6}\Big[(A^3 - A)\,M_i + (B^3 - B)\,M_{i+1}\Big]

At x_i: A = 1, B = 0, the bracket is 0, so S = y_i. Values and S'' are continuous by construction.
If all M_i = 0 this is piecewise linear: the bracket is the curvature correction.
Only the continuity of S' is left to impose: one equation per interior point.


This is the standard trick (as in Numerical Recipes): choose unknowns that make most conditions automatic. Interpolation and continuity of S’’ are built in, so only n - 2 slope conditions remain, plus two end conditions: n equations for the n values M_i. A and B are the weights of linear interpolation; they go from 1 to 0 and 0 to 1 across the interval. Students do not need to derive the formula; they need to see that it passes through the points and that M_i is its second derivative there.

title: Splines
text:
Continuous slope → a tridiagonal system
Setting S' from the left equal to S' from the right at each interior x_i gives
h_{i-1}\,M_{i-1} + 2(h_{i-1} + h_i)\,M_i + h_i\,M_{i+1} = 6\left(\frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{h_i} - \frac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\right)
Each equation involves only three neighbours. Example: 4 points (0,0), (1,1), (2,0), (3,1), h = 1, natural ends M_1 = M_4 = 0:
\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} M_2 \\ M_3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6(-1 - 1) \\ 6(1 + 1)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -12 \\ 12\end{pmatrix} \quad\Rightarrow\quad M_2 = -4,\; M_3 = 4

Tridiagonal, symmetric, and strictly diagonally dominant: 2(h_{i-1} + h_i) > h_{i-1} + h_i.
So the Thomas algorithm from Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse solves it in O(n), with no pivoting needed.


The right-hand side is 6 times the change in slope of the data at x_i: a second difference. Where the data bend down (point 2) the curvature M is negative; where they bend up, positive. By hand: subtract a quarter of row 1 from row 2: 3.75 M3 = 12 + 3 = 15, M3 = 4, then M2 = (-12 - 4)/4 = -4. That is the Thomas forward sweep and back substitution. Diagonal dominance holds for any spacing, which is why spline codes never pivot. For a million points the solve takes milliseconds.

title: Splines
text:
A natural spline in R
natural_M <- function(x, y) {                # second derivatives, M_1 = M_n = 0
  n <- length(x); h <- diff(x); s <- diff(y) / h
  hl <- h[-(n - 1)]; hr <- h[-1]             # h_{i-1} and h_i, i = 2..n-1
  c(0, thomas(hl, 2 * (hl + hr), hr, 6 * diff(s)), 0)
}
spline_eval <- function(x, y, M, t) {
  i <- findInterval(t, x, all.inside = TRUE) # which interval is t in?
  h <- x[i + 1] - x[i]; A <- (x[i + 1] - t) / h; B <- (t - x[i]) / h
  A * y[i] + B * y[i + 1] + ((A^3 - A) * M[i] + (B^3 - B) * M[i + 1]) * h^2 / 6
}
natural_M(c(0, 1, 2, 3), c(0, 1, 0, 1))
# [1]  0 -4  4  0

thomas(a, b, c, d) is the function from Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse (sub-, main, super-diagonal, right-hand side).
findInterval finds the interval of each t by binary search.


Eight lines plus Thomas. diff(s) is the change in slope, the right-hand side. thomas expects four vectors of the same length and ignores a[1] and c[n], so passing hl and hr directly works: the first entry of hl and the last of hr are not used. The exercise adds the derivative formula and the clamped variant. This is the “write it yourself first” step; next slide we compare with the library.

title: Splines
text:
Check against the library
M <- natural_M(t, y)                          # the 41 noisy OD reads
f <- splinefun(t, y, method = "natural")      # R's natural spline
tt <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.01)
max(abs(spline_eval(t, y, M, tt) - f(tt)))
# [1] 2.220446e-16
f(3.1); f(3.1, deriv = 1)                     # value and slope at 3.1 h
# [1] 0.4073834
# [1] 0.2608974

splinefun returns a function; deriv = 1, 2, 3 gives the derivatives of the spline.
Agreement to rounding level: our 8 lines and R’s compiled code solve the same tridiagonal system.
Check for your own spline: it passes through the data, and S' from the left equals S' from the right at every x_i.


splinefun is the function-returning version; spline() returns points on a grid. Note the slope: 0.261 OD per hour at 3.1 h, but the true growth rate there is 0.216. The spline is exact in its arithmetic and still gives a poor slope, because it goes through every noisy point. Keep that in mind; we come back to it after the boundary conditions.

title: Splines
section: Boundary conditions: the two missing equations
text:
Boundary conditions: the two missing equations








name
condition at each end
when to use




natural
S'' = 0: M_1 = M_n = 0
no information about the ends


clamped
S' = a known slope, f'(x_1), f'(x_n)
slope known (e.g. a plateau: S' = 0)


not-a-knot
S''' continuous at x_2 and x_{n-1}
default in Python and MATLAB




Clamped, left end: 2h_1 M_1 + h_1 M_2 = 6\left(\frac{y_2 - y_1}{h_1} - f'(x_1)\right). Still tridiagonal.
Not-a-knot: the first two pieces are one cubic. The system is no longer exactly tridiagonal, but still O(n).
R’s default, method = "fmm" (Forsythe, Malcolm, Moler), fits a cubic to the first and last 4 points and matches its S''' at each end.


Natural is the free end of the draughtsman’s strip: no bending at the ends. It is correct only if the true function has zero curvature at the ends, which is rarely the case. Clamped is best when you really know the slope, and wrong when you guess it: setting S’ = 0 at the start of a growth curve that is already growing makes things worse, the exercise shows it. Not-a-knot and fmm both use the data near the end to guess the end behaviour; they give fourth-order accuracy everywhere. R has no clamped option in splinefun; pracma::cubicspline(endp2nd = TRUE, der = …) does it, or modify the first and last rows of your own system.

title: Splines
text:
Boundary conditions: what they change


11 exact OD values, h = 1 h. Away from the ends all three agree.
Natural forces S''(0) = 0, but N''(0) = 0.028: the error near t = 0 is about 5× larger than anywhere else.


The error curves are spline minus the true logistic. The interior error has the same shape for all three, because the influence of an end condition decays by a factor of about 3.7 per interval (the ratio of the diagonal to the off-diagonal in the tridiagonal system). Only the first one or two intervals see the difference. Clamped with the true slopes, and not-a-knot, are both accurate at the ends. If what you care about is the start of the growth curve (the lag phase), the boundary condition matters.

title: Splines
text:
Same data, different defaults
x <- 0:4; y5 <- c(0, 1, 0, 1, 0)
splinefun(x, y5)(0.5)                        # R default: "fmm"
# [1] 1.055556
splinefun(x, y5, method = "natural")(0.5)
# [1] 0.7678571

end condition

Python CubicSpline(x, y, bc_type="natural")

Check: when an R and a Python result differ near the ends, look at the end conditions first.

Wildly oscillating data exaggerate the difference, but the point holds: three defaults, three answers in the first interval, all “correct”. In the interior they agree closely. When porting an analysis from MATLAB or Python to R, or comparing with a colleague’s numbers, check the end condition. scipy.interpolate.CubicSpline takes bc_type = “natural”, “not-a-knot”, “clamped” (slope 0), or explicit ((1, slope_left), (1, slope_right)).

title: Splines
section: How fast does the error fall?
text:
How fast does the error fall?


Exact OD values on a grid of spacing h. Slopes read off as in Convergence and cost: linear O(h^2), cubic spline O(h^4), its derivative O(h^3).
Natural ends drop the spline to O(h^2): the error at t = 0 dominates.


Halving h: piecewise linear error divides by 4, the fmm spline by 16, the spline’s slope by 8. For smooth data a cubic spline with good end conditions is very accurate: at h = 0.25 h (a 15-minute plate reader), the error is 1e-6 OD, far below any measurement noise. The natural spline has the right slope (4) in the interior but the end error is O(h^2) because it imposes a wrong curvature there; its constant is small here because N’’(0) is small. This is the error plot every method in the course gets. It assumes exact data. With noisy data, the error does not go to zero as h shrinks, as the next slides show.

title: Splines
text:
Failure: overshoot


After a steep drop the cubic swings below the data: -1.6 TPM at 3 h. Negative expression.
Fixes: a monotone interpolant (splinefun(method = "monoH.FC"), Python PchipInterpolator), or interpolate \log_2 expression and transform back.
Check: plot the interpolant on a fine grid; look for values outside the range of neighbouring data.


Continuity of S’’ is a strong requirement: a curve that comes down steeply and must flatten out with continuous curvature has to swing past. Piecewise linear never overshoots. A monotone cubic (Fritsch-Carlson in R’s monoH.FC, Fritsch-Butland in PCHIP) chooses the slopes at the data points so that each piece stays between its two values; it gives up continuity of S’’. Interpolating on the log scale guarantees positive values but can overshoot the peak upwards, here to 48 TPM instead of 40. There is no free lunch: decide which property matters (positivity, monotonicity, smoothness) and check it.

title: Splines
text:
Interpolating noisy data
An interpolating spline goes through every point, noise included.
rms <- function(e) sqrt(mean(e^2))
rate <- function(t) r * od(t) * (1 - od(t) / K)     # true growth rate
rms(cd - rate(t[2:(n - 1)]))                       # central differences
# [1] 0.02427257
f <- splinefun(t, y, method = "natural")
rms(f(t, deriv = 1) - rate(t))                     # slope of interpolating spline
# [1] 0.03827564

The spline’s slope is worse than plain central differences: it bends to hit every noisy point.
With exact data the spline was accurate to 10^{-6}; with noise sd 0.01 it is wrong by 0.04. More points (smaller h) do not help.


This is the same lesson as in Convergence and cost: dividing differences of noisy numbers by small numbers amplifies noise. There the noise was rounding, 1e-16; here it is the plate reader, 1e-2. The O(h^4) convergence of the previous slide is about the truncation error of the method; it says nothing about noise. To get a good slope we must give up passing through the data.

title: Splines
text:
Smoothing splines
Among all smooth curves f, choose the one that minimises
\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - f(t_i)\big)^2}_{\text{misfit}} \;+\; \lambda \underbrace{\int \big(f''(t)\big)^2\,dt}_{\text{roughness}}

\lambda = 0: only the misfit counts → the interpolating natural spline.
\lambda \to \infty: no curvature allowed → the least-squares straight line.
The minimiser is always a natural cubic spline with knots at the data points. Finding it is a banded linear system (O(n), as before).
R: smooth.spline; Python: scipy.interpolate.make_smoothing_spline.


Penalised least squares: a misfit term like in Least squares, plus a penalty on roughness. This is the same idea as ridge regularisation in The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation, with the penalty on curvature instead of on coefficient size. The surprising theorem (Reinsch 1967) is that the best curve is a natural cubic spline, so the infinite-dimensional problem becomes a linear system for n values. In the Reinsch form it is pentadiagonal, (R + lambda Q^T Q) gamma = Q^T y, with R tridiagonal and Q with three non-zeros per column. The exercise builds it in Rust. Units: lambda has units of (OD)^2 times hours^3, so its size depends on the units of t; R rescales t to [0, 1] internally, Python does not, so Python’s lam = R’s lambda times (range of t)^3.

title: Splines
text:
The bias–noise trade-off


Small \lambda (df = 30): follows the noise; the slope is useless. Large \lambda (df = 4): too stiff; it cuts the peak growth rate (bias).
df (equivalent degrees of freedom): from 2 (a line) to n (interpolation). Easier to read than \lambda.


Top row: the fitted OD curves; bottom row: their derivatives against the true growth rate (dashed). On the OD scale all three look acceptable, which is why you must look at the quantity you actually want. Too little smoothing: variance (noise) dominates. Too much: bias dominates, the peak rate is flattened and moved, and the start and end are wrong. df is the trace of the hat matrix, the matrix that maps data y to fitted values; for a regression with p parameters it equals p. It is the number you should report with a smoothing spline fit.

title: Splines
text:
Choosing \lambda: cross-validation and GCV
Leave-one-out CV: leave point i out, fit, predict y_i; minimise the mean squared prediction error. For a smoother with hat matrix A (\hat{\mathbf y} = A\mathbf y) no refit is needed: \text{CV}(\lambda) = \frac1n \sum_i \left(\frac{y_i - \hat y_i}{1 - A_{ii}}\right)^2, \qquad \text{GCV}(\lambda) = \frac{n\,\text{RSS}}{(n - \text{df})^2}, \quad \text{df} = \operatorname{tr} A
fit <- smooth.spline(t, y)                    # lambda chosen by GCV (default)
fit
# Smoothing Parameter  spar= 0.565132  lambda= 0.0001355283 (14 iterations)
# Equivalent Degrees of Freedom (Df): 9.416379
# Penalized Criterion (RSS): 0.002053709
# GCV: 8.4411e-05

GCV replaces each A_{ii} by the average \text{df}/n: cheaper, and less sensitive to single points. cv = TRUE gives ordinary CV (df = 9.8 here).


The idea: a good lambda predicts data you have not used. Leave-one-out needs n refits in principle, but for any linear smoother the left-out residual is the ordinary residual divided by 1 - A_ii, so one fit suffices. GCV (Craven and Wahba 1979) averages the leverages. Check the GCV formula on the output: 41 * 0.002054 / (41 - 9.416)^2 = 8.44e-5. Python’s make_smoothing_spline(t, y) with lam = None also uses GCV and gives the same curve. smooth.spline searches over spar, a log-scale reparametrisation of lambda, with a one-dimensional optimiser (as in Optimisation in one dimension).

title: Splines
text:
GCV against the true error


Left: GCV score over a grid of \lambda (shown as df). Right: the true rms error of the growth rate, which we know only because the data are simulated.
The GCV minimum (df = 9.4) is near the best df for the slope. That is luck as much as design: GCV optimises the curve, not its derivative.


Right panel is the bias-noise trade-off as a curve: error falls as df rises from 3 (bias shrinks), then rises again (noise). The bottom of the U is where the two are balanced. GCV is flat over a range of df, which is typical: any df from about 8 to 14 gives a similar fit. For derivatives, the theory says slightly more smoothing than the GCV choice is often better, because differentiation amplifies the noise more than the bias. Report the df you used, and try a few values around it to see that your conclusions do not depend on it.

title: Splines
section: Growth rate from the smoothed curve
text:
Growth rate from the smoothed curve

g <- predict(fit, tf, deriv = 1)$y            # tf: fine grid, 0 to 10 h
c(max(g), tf[which.max(g)])                   # true: 0.24 at 3.92 h
# [1] 0.2388003 4.0100000

RMS error of the growth rate: central differences 0.024, interpolating spline 0.038, smoothing spline 0.0067.


predict.smooth.spline with deriv = 1 returns the slope of the fitted spline. The maximum growth rate is estimated within 0.5 % and its time within 6 minutes. Note the ends: the smoothing spline is natural, so S’’ = 0 at both ends, which biases the slope near t = 0 and t = 10 (visible at the left end). If you have a model, for example the logistic, fitting it directly (Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting, Part 9) uses that knowledge and does better; a smoothing spline is what you use when you do not want to assume a model.

title: Splines
text:
Biology: expression along pseudotime


300 cells, ordered by pseudotime; one gene, noisy. smooth.spline(pt, ex): df = 12.9; peak at pseudotime 0.602 (true 0.6).
Same tool as the trend fits in single-cell trajectory packages (tradeSeq, Monocle), which fit a spline trend per gene.


Pseudotime orders cells along a differentiation trajectory; each gene is a noisy function of pseudotime, with many cells but large cell-to-cell noise. Smoothing splines (or regression splines with fewer knots) are the standard way to get a trend, find where a gene peaks, or test whether it changes along the trajectory. With thousands of cells, smooth.spline uses fewer knots than data points (nknots) to keep the system small; the trade-off is the same. The exercise does this with 40 cells and compares GCV with leave-one-out CV.

title: Splines
text:
Failure: GCV with correlated noise


Here the reads drift (each error is 0.9 × the previous one plus new noise, as with condensation or settling cells). GCV sees the drift as signal: df = 26.9, a wiggly slope.
GCV assumes independent errors. Check: lag-1 correlation of the residuals (acf); here -0.60. Use replicate wells, or fix df by hand.


Correlated errors are common in time series: one well measured repeatedly, or neighbouring cells in pseudotime sharing a batch. GCV cannot tell slow noise from signal, so it undersmooths. The residual check: strongly negative lag-1 correlation means the fit follows the noise (here -0.60; for the GCV fit to the independent-noise OD data of the earlier slides it is -0.18); strongly positive means runs of residuals with the same sign, i.e. bias from oversmoothing. For a real experiment the best check is biological replicates: a smoothing parameter that gives growth rates that differ between replicate wells by more than their noise is too small.

title: Splines
text:
R and Python
